#10363. Introducing Falcon-H1-Arabic: Pushing the Boundaries of Arabic Language AI with Hybrid Architecture

Discover more in our official blogpost, featuring an interactive experience

The journey of building world-class Arabic language models has been one of continuous learning and iteration. Today, we're excited to announce Falcon-H1-Arabic, our most advanced Arabic language model family to date, representing a significant leap forward in both architecture and capabilities. This release embodies months of research, community feedback, and technical innovation, culminating in three powerful models that set new standards for Arabic natural language processing.

When we launched Falcon-Arabic a few months ago, the response from the community was both humbling and enlightening. Developers, researchers and students across the Arab world used the model for real use cases, pushing them to its limits and providing invaluable feedback. We learned where the model excelled and, more importantly, where it struggled. Long-context understanding, dialectal variations, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific knowledge emerged as key areas requiring deeper attention.

We didn't just want to make incremental improvements, we wanted to fundamentally rethink our approach. The result is Falcon-H1-Arabic, a model family that addresses every piece of feedback we received while introducing architectural innovations that were previously unexplored in Arabic language modeling.

Falcon-H1-Arabic 3B, 7B, 34B models outperforming all SOTA models of similar sizes and sometimes bigger.

Falcon-H1-Arabic is built on the Falcon-H1 hybrid architecture, which integrates State Space Models (Mamba) and Transformer attention within every block. Both components run in parallel and their representations are fused before the block’s output projection. This design provides the linear-time scalability of Mamba for extremely long sequences while preserving the precise long-range modeling capabilities of attention. For Arabic, with its rich morphology and flexible sentence structures, this approach significantly improves coherence and reasoning across extended text. We've deployed this architecture across three scales (3B, 7B, 34B parameters), each balancing capacity, efficiency, and deployability for different use cases from edge devices to enterprise applications.

Falcon-H1 architecture. Attention and SSM run in parallel within each block; their outputs are concatenated before the block’s output projection. The number of SSM/Attention heads depends on the model size. More details on the Falcon-H1 technical report.

We've dramatically increased context capabilities from Falcon-Arabic's 32K limit to 128K tokens for the 3B model and 256K tokens for both the 7B and 34B models. At 256K tokens (~200,000 words), these models can process several novels or hundreds of pages of technical documentation enabling applications in legal analysis, medical records, academic research, and extended conversations that were previously impractical. Our post-training specifically addresses "lost in the middle" challenges to ensure models effectively utilize their full context range, not just accept long inputs.

We rebuilt our pre-training data pipeline from the ground up to better reflect the complexity of Arabic. This began with a multi-stage quality filtering process tailored to Arabic orthography, morphology, diacritics, and syntactic patterns. Instead of heuristic filtering, we used deep linguistic analysis to isolate coherent, well-structured text and remove noise commonly found in open-web corpora. The result is a significantly cleaner, more stylistically consistent Arabic dataset.

Dialect coverage was another key priority. Arabic is not monolithic; Modern Standard Arabic coexists with dialects such as Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, and Maghrebi, each with distinct vocabularies and grammatical constructions. We expanded dialectal sources substantially so the models would understand and generate the full spectrum of real-world Arabic rather than leaning disproportionately toward formal MSA. To maintain global reasoning and domain diversity, we also preserved the multilingual capabilities of Falcon-H1 by training the Arabic models on an almost equal mix of Arabic, English, and multilingual content totalling around 300 Billion Tokens. This ensures strong performance in code, STEM, and cross-lingual reasoning. The following figure illustrates the distribution of the pre-training data across languages and categories. All values are expressed in billions of tokens.

After pre-training, Falcon-H1-Arabic undergoes a focused post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). During SFT, we expose the models to high-quality Arabic instructions, curated long-context examples, and structured reasoning tasks that teach them to follow directives, maintain coherence over extended sequences, and ground their responses in relevant information. This stage is crucial for ensuring that the models can actually use their large context windows which does not emerge automatically from architecture alone.

We follow SFT with a targeted DPO phase to refine alignment, conversational quality, and preference consistency. DPO helps the models balance long-context reasoning with general linguistic competence, improving helpfulness and reducing common failure modes such as drifting, overuse of context, or neglecting earlier information. Throughout both stages, we carefully monitor for catastrophic forgetting and maintain a controlled curriculum so gains in long-context behavior do not come at the expense of core reasoning or factual accuracy. The result is a family of models that handles extended documents and dialogue with ease while preserving strong performance on everyday language tasks.

Beyond benchmark-oriented optimization, our post-training process deliberately strengthens areas that traditional evaluations do not fully capture, including conversational faithfulness, rhetorical organization, structured follow-ups, and discourse coherence. These enhancements significantly boost the model’s practical usefulness, making Falcon-H1-Arabic more dependable in real multi-turn dialogue, instruction execution, and long-context conversational flows.

Numbers tell an important part of the story. On the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard (OALL), a comprehensive benchmark evaluating Arabic language understanding across diverse tasks, Falcon-H1-Arabic achieves state-of-the-art results at every scale we tested. Note that our scores may vary slightly from those reported on the leaderboard, as we used vLLM as the backend instead of the leaderboard’s Accelerate-based implementation. These differences are typically under one point while offering significantly faster runtime.

Beyond OALL, we also report results on the 3LM benchmark for STEM-related tasks on both synthetic and native splits; Arabculture for Arabic culture assessment; and AraDice for Arabic dialect coverage across Levantine, and Egyptian varieties as well as Arabic culture across 6 countries. The reported AraDice score is the average of all the 3 scores.

Starting with the 3B model, the performance is exceptional. It reaches approximately 62% on OALL, outperforming all small-scale models, including Gemma-4B, Qwen3-4B, and Phi-4-mini by roughly ten points. On 3LM, the main Arabic STEM benchmark, it scores around 82% on the native split and 73% on the synthetic split. It also achieves about 62% on the ArabCulture benchmark and around 50% across AraDice dialect evaluation (Egyptian, Gulf, and Levantine). This makes Falcon-H1-Arabic-3B a high-quality, highly efficient model suitable for edge deployments, real-time applications, and agentic systems where latency and cost matter.

The 7B model continues this upward trajectory. With a score of 71.7% on OALL, it surpasses all models in the ~10B class, including Fanar-9B, Allam-7B*, and Qwen3-8B. On 3LM, it reaches about 92% on the native split and 85% on the synthetic one. AraDice scores rise into the mid-50s across all dialects, and ArabCulture results approach 80%. This model strikes an ideal balance between capability and deployability, making it the most practical choice for general-purpose Arabic NLP in production environments.

The 34B model represents our flagship system and establishes a new state of the art for Arabic language modeling. It reaches approximately 75% on OALL, outperforming not only models of similar size but even much larger systems such as Llama-3.3-70B and AceGPT2-32B. Its 3LM scores reach about 96% on the native split and 94% on the synthetic one. On ArabCulture it scores close to 80%, and on AraDice it reaches around 53 across dialects. The fact that a 34B hybrid model surpasses the performance of 70B-scale transformers demonstrates the effectiveness of the Falcon-H1 architecture, the quality of the data, and the strength of the post-training pipeline.

These benchmark results validate our approach but also highlight an important reality: the frontier of Arabic language modeling is advancing rapidly. Each percentage point on these benchmarks represents countless hours of engineering effort, careful dataset curation, and architectural refinement. The margins by which Falcon-H1-Arabic leads aren't just statistical artifacts, they translate to meaningfully better user experiences in real-world applications.

Each model in the Falcon-H1-Arabic family is suited to different deployment scenarios. The 3B model is optimized for speed, cost-efficiency, and high-throughput systems, making it ideal for agentic workflows, on-device applications, low-latency chat, and environments with strict resource constraints. The 7B model serves as the general-purpose workhorse for most production applications, powering document understanding systems, chatbots, summarization pipelines, and content generation tools. The 34B model is designed for high-stakes domains where accuracy and long-range reasoning matter most, including legal analysis, medical summarization, academic research, and large-scale enterprise automation. Its extended context window makes it uniquely capable of analyzing hundreds of pages of text in a single pass while maintaining precise coherence.

Like all language models, Falcon-H1-Arabic may reflect biases from training data and can produce hallucinated information. Model outputs should not be used as sole authorities for medical, legal, or financial decisions without professional verification. Long-context performance may degrade at extreme ranges. We recommend task-specific evaluation and appropriate guardrails before deployment in production or sensitive applications.

This work stands on the shoulders of many. We extend our gratitude to the Arabic NLP research community, whose open sharing of benchmarks, datasets, and methodologies enables progress across the field. Special thanks to our colleagues at TII: Ilyas Chahed, Younes Belkada, Dhia Eddine Rhaiem, Puneesh Khanna, Jingwei Zuo, Mikhail Lubinets, Slim Frikha, Maksim Velikanov, Kacper Piskorski, and Suhail Mohmad for their invaluable support during this project.

Track, rank and evaluate open Arabic LLMs and chatbots

Impressive milestone for Arabic language AI. Falcon-H1-Arabic’s hybrid architecture is a strong step toward closing the performance gap in high-quality Arabic understanding and generation. Exciting to see innovation that’s not just scaling models, but rethinking architecture to better capture the richness and complexity of Arabic. Looking forward to seeing real-world applications and benchmarks. https://soch.sindhwildlife.com.pk/

Amazon’s closure email cites a verification process and offers no reason.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI creator Nick Saraev says on X that Amazon closed his account after he tried to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark AI mini-PCs. The closure email cites a verification process and gives no reason. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney chimed in that his regular orders would go through, then get canceled before arrival, after he tried to buy two GPUs.

Update: Amazon just closed my account.Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist. Be careful!November 1, 2026

Saraev puts it plainly that “Amazon just closed my account” and that “Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist.” He was “4 orders deep,” and Amazon will no longer allow him to buy DGX Sparks.

The shared screenshots indicate those orders were all canceled, with each stating, “Your order was canceled. You have not been charged for this order.” Although he does not give a unit count, the screenshots indicate he tried to buy seven DGX Sparks in total. All show the same listing, with 128GB of memory and 4TB of storage.

Amazon’s support account did respond to his earlier post, about three hours before his closure post, offering a review. The shared email shows that Amazon had “made the final decision” to close his account after review; no reason was given. However, it did mention “previous attempts to verify your account,” and he says he did go through the verification process, but seven DGX Sparks is a significant amount that might draw suspicion. Either way, Amazon’s Conditions of Use reserve the right to “refuse service, terminate accounts” or “cancel orders in its sole discretion.”

He’s not alone in running into trouble with the company. Sweeney says that “Amazon didn’t cancel my account but continued accepting all my regular orders and canceling them just prior to arrival dates, after I tried to buy two NVIDIA GPUs. Rather bizarre.” Nvidia GPUs are often used for local inference. Saraev replied that everyone would “appreciate a bit more transparency.”

Also, in September, Dracones89 on the Nvidia developer forum shared that one Amazon account was hit with “suspicious activity locks” while trying to buy a pair of Asus GX10s; the user ended up with two DGX Sparks from Micro Center instead. Another X user, @PurzBeats, wrote, “They canceled the order when I tried to buy my 5090, twice.” This is a different trajectory than the OpenClaw days of Mac minis, when buyers faced long delivery waits rather than canceled orders or closed accounts.

With local inference remaining of high interest to many, particularly AI influencers, the event is potentially disturbing, especially after recent comments about self-owned DRAM by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. While this time it was a guy who helps entrepreneurs and small businesses implement AI and claims 500K on YouTube and 700K on Instagram, the slope is slippery, although Saraev’s orders are hardly typical.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The 128GB DGX Spark has an MSRP of $6,950, but it may be found at 20% or more over that: two Amazon listings showed $8,499.99 and $9,499.99 when we checked today, which would put seven at roughly $59,500 to $66,500. Both showed Prime delivery tomorrow, so the hardware is still on sale there.

Hardware has been climbing in price, largely due to rising memory costs. As open-weight models have become more popular, so has local AI inference. The combination may make retailers uneasy, as you’re dealing with high ticket prices and there has been uncertainty about the safety of models as they have improved, with open-source AI agent tools reportedly being used in multiple recent cybersecurity incidents.

Micro Center, a different retailer, required one buyer to sign an Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration with photo ID, end user, and an install location, just for a workstation with an RTX 5090. This form specifically forbade exporting or reselling the hardware, which might give a little insight into Amazon’s reasoning, too. Amazon’s conditions also say customers “must comply with all U.S. or other export and re-export restrictions.” China and the U.S. remain locked in a fight over exports of AI hardware.

Amazon hasn’t explained itself, but the attention this is getting may motivate a more detailed response. Right now, it’s a warning signal to users looking to buy significant amounts of hardware for AI work, at least from traditional online retailers. Brick-and-mortar stores, like Micro Center, may crack down further to prevent workarounds designed to export the hardware illegally.

#10361. SBOMs Alone Can't Reveal the Scope of a Supply Chain Attack

A recent Shai-Hulud attack shows defenders need real-time visibility into production code and affected services to respond to supply chain compromises.

ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — Depending on a software bill of materials (SBOM) to determine what happens when a malicious package slips past security checks can leave defenders struggling to establish what code actually executed, which systems it touched, and how far the compromise spread.

In a session at the ISC2 Security Congress 2026 this week, Atlassian product security manager Deepam Kanjani used a real-world compromise involving the Shai-Hulud worm to highlight incident response challenges, including gaps in runtime visibility, transitive dependency ownership, and attacker attribution.

In the session, Kanjani said he had altered all identifying details, figures, and the sequence of events to protect confidentiality, though his first-person, war-room narrative of underlying attack techniques, technical behaviors, and challenges was based on real events at a large-scale software-as-a-service (SaaS) environment.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Kanjani described the incident as involving a package that appeared legitimate, with a matching SHA hash, more than 3,400 GitHub stars, and a repository that looked credible to the company's security tooling. But hidden three layers deep in the package was a malicious transitive dependency named shai-hulud, after the giant sandworms in the Dune movie series. Because it was not a direct dependency, it did not surface in a top-level dependency audit.

The first inkling that something was wrong came when a behavioral scanner flagged the package as running something it shouldn't have been running. Incident responders initially dismissed the alert as a likely false positive because the hash matched and there was no other obvious indication of the package being malicious.

Additionally, the SBOM reported the environment as clean when the security team consulted it. What they did not realize at the time was that the SBOM was two development sprints out of date, Kanjani said.

As the response unfolded, the team could not say with confidence which services used the package. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided initial clues but could not establish which services were affected or how far the compromise had spread. Responders needed runtime evidence to determine what code had actually executed and what it could access.

Without that runtime telemetry, they had to correlate logs manually across more than 400 services, leaving them without a reliable picture of the compromise's potential reach. An initial Slack message from the incident response handler to enterprise stakeholders made matters worse by being too vague and prompting a set of parallel investigations into the still-unfolding event.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

The security team's efforts to identify the attacker by tracing registry ownership, npm maintainer history, publisher identities, and GitHub records quickly led them to dead ends. The repository had been copied from a legitimate project, and the publisher's identity and account history appeared to have been fabricated, Kanjani said.

Researchers have subsequently attributed at least some of the later Shai-Hulud attacks to a threat actor tracked as TeamPCP.

The key takeaway, according to Kanjani, is that organizations need to look beyond SBOMs and dependency inventories and instead base incident response around what actually runs in production. The focus should be to equip security teams to identify, scope, prioritize, and contain incidents and enable real-time visibility into affected services and the potential scope of a compromise.

"You are triaging a runtime graph. Not a dependency file. Your tools must reflect that," he said.

Kanjani recommended that organizations keep deployed SBOMs under 72 hours old and try to ensure that more than 98% of production services meet that threshold. He also recommended enabling runtime capabilities to detect unknown module loads in under 90 seconds and daily registry checks to detect lookalikes of internal package names within 24 hours of publication.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

Kanjani described these as targets that organizations should calibrate for their own environments rather than as universal benchmarks. In addition, security teams should focus on the operation rather than the operator, Kanjani said. "Identity signals rotate. Operational necessities don't. Build detection around what the worm must do to function — not who's driving it."

All communications with stakeholders regarding a security incident also need to be direct and unambiguous. The key is to be honest, he said, while making sure to present the details in language appropriate for the intended audience.

"Don't bullsh-t. Tell them the reality in a way they can absorb it," he said. "You don't want to sell panic."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#10359. NVIDIA Cosmos Reason 2 Brings Advanced Reasoning To Physical AI

NVIDIA today released Cosmos Reason 2, the latest advancement in open, reasoning vision language models for physical AI. Cosmos Reason 2 surpasses its previous version in accuracy and tops the Physical AI Bench and Physical Reasoning leaderboards as the #1 open model for visual understanding.

Since their introduction, vision-language models have rapidly improved at tasks like object and pattern recognition in images. But they still struggle with tasks humans find natural, like planning several steps ahead, dealing with uncertainty or adapting to new situations. Cosmos Reason is designed to close this gap by giving robots and AI agents stronger common sense and reasoning to solve complex problems step by step.

Cosmos Reason 2 is a state-of-the-art, open reasoning vision-language model (VLM) that enables robots and AI agents to see, understand, plan, and act in the physical world like humans. It uses common sense, physics, and prior knowledge to recognize how objects move across space and time to handle complex tasks, adapt to new situations, and figure out how to solve problems step by step.

Improved spatio-temporal understanding and timestamp precision.

Optimized performance with flexible deployment options from edge to cloud with 2B and 8B parameters model sizes.

Support for expanded set of spatial understanding and visual perception capabilities — 2D/3D point localization, bounding box coordinates, trajectory data, and OCR support.

Improved long-context understanding with 256K input tokens, up from 16K with Cosmos Reason 1.

Adaptable to multiple use cases with easy-to-use Cosmos Cookbook recipes.

Video analytics AI agents — These agents can extract valuable insights from massive volumes of video data to optimize processes. Cosmos Reason 2 builds on the capabilities of Cosmos Reason 1 and now provides OCR support, as well as 2D/3D point localization and a set of mark understanding.

Developers can jumpstart development of video analytics AI agents by using the NVIDIA blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Salesforce is transforming workplace safety and compliance by analyzing video footage captured by Cobalt robots with Agentforce and VSS blueprint with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Data annotation and critique — Enable developers to automate high-quality annotation and critique of massive, diverse training datasets. Cosmos Reason provides time stamps and detailed descriptions for real or synthetically generated training videos.

Uber is exploring Cosmos Reason 2 to deliver accurate, searchable video captions for autonomous vehicle (AV) training data, enabling efficient identification of critical driving scenarios. This co-authored Reason 2 for AV Video Captioning and VQA recipe demonstrates how to fine-tune and evaluate Cosmos Reason 2-8B on annotated AV videos. Across multiple evaluation metrics, measurable improvements were achieved: BLEU scores improved 10.6% (0.113 → 0.125), MCQ-based VQA gained 0.67 percentage points (80.18% → 80.85%), and LingoQA increased 13.8% (63.2% → 77.0%). These gains demonstrate effective domain adaptation for AV applications.

Robot planning and reasoning — Act as the brain for deliberate, methodical decision-making in a robot vision language action (VLA) model. Cosmos Reason 2 now provides trajectory coordinates in addition to determining next steps.

Encord provides native support for Cosmos Reason 2 in its Data Agent library and AI data platform, enabling developers to leverage Cosmos Reason 2 as a VLA for robotics and other physical AI use cases.

Companies like Hitachi, Milestone and VAST Data are using Cosmos Reason to advance robotics, autonomous driving, and video analytics AI agents for traffic and workplace safety.

Try Cosmos Reason 2 on build.nvidia.com and experience the latest features with sample prompts for generating bounding boxes and robot trajectories. Upload your own videos and images for further analysis.

Download Cosmos Reason 2 models (2B and 8B) on Hugging Face or use Cosmos Reason 2 in the cloud. The model will be available soon on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. To get started, check out Cosmos Reason 2 documentation and the Cosmos Cookbook.

Cosmos Predict is a generative AI model that predicts future states of the physical world as video, based on text, image, or video inputs.

Cosmos Transfer is our lightest multicontrol model built for video to world style transfer.

NVIDIA GR00T N1.6 is an open reasoning vision language action (VLA) model, purpose-built for humanoid robots, that unlocks full body control and uses NVIDIA Cosmos Reason for better reasoning and contextual understanding.

#10357. AI, DevOps and the Cost of Hosting: From Idea to Production for $0

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An AI coding agent rebuilt my photo-collage app as a distributed system and deployed it to a free server. The hard part turned out to be hardware: one free ARM CPU, 538 collages created during load testing, zero failed jobs, and $0 a month.

Like most developers, I have never been short of product ideas. Hosting them has always been the problem. I have tried shared hosting with SmartWeb, Azure free credits, Google Compute Engine’s free VM instances, SmartWeb’s virtual private servers, and Heroku dynos. None of them left me satisfied. The worst experience was a $200 charge for an AI address API on Google Cloud—for an application that never earned me a single kobo.

I am not a cheapskate, but I learned quickly that one of the easiest ways to kill a potentially good idea is to get the finances wrong. An application has to stay online until it reaches a critical mass of users, and hosting an untested, unverified product on expensive hardware can be wasteful.

Agentic AI coding has changed how quickly I can move from idea to production. Over about five weeks of intermittent coding—amounting to roughly three days of full work with Claude—my photo-stitching app went from an Angular 8 project that would not even build to a distributed system running in production.

Along the way, Claude upgraded the front end from Angular 8 to Angular 22 and fixed the build on Node 24. It set up RabbitMQ with Docker Compose so the message broker configures itself on startup, and added real-time notifications over SignalR with a progress spinner. It fixed a crash loop caused by an unreadable iPhone photo. It redesigned the system so any server can process any job, with switchable database and file storage, direct browser-to-storage uploads, and photos resized in the browser before upload. It added reliability work that a team might debate for a sprint: a dead-letter queue, confirmed publishing, idempotent workers, recovery of stuck jobs, and automatic clean-up. It fixed the stitching so photos keep their proportions and borders are even. It wrote 41 automated tests and scrubbed leaked passwords and personal photos from the Git history.

Coding, QA, DevOps, and production support used to be separate phases, often handled by separate people. Here they happened in one conversation. When code becomes this cheap to produce, the bottleneck moves. For me, it moved to hardware.

To check what the AI builds, you have to run it locally. A distributed app means running the whole system locally: a web app, a background worker, a message broker, a database, and storage emulators. Because Claude adds features quickly, and each one can add another container, it is easy to exhaust a laptop’s RAM and CPU.

My setup made this lesson concrete. I work on a MacBook Air, with Visual Studio in a Windows virtual machine. Docker cannot run inside that VM on Apple Silicon, so Claude ran Docker on the Mac and drove it from Windows over SSH. Later, my mobile connection started dropping large packets and broke uploads from the VM, so Claude moved the load testing onto the server itself. The software problems took minutes. The hardware and network problems took longer.

Then comes hosting. Heroku looked like the easy route, but it has had no free dynos since 2022. The cheapest option is an Eco dyno at about $5 a month, plus about $5 for Postgres. That is affordable, but running it for an idea that has no users yet did not seem prudent.

Claude suggested Oracle Cloud’s Always Free tier: an ARM server with up to 4 CPUs and 24 GB of RAM, free with no end date. I created a small instance with 1 CPU and about 6 GB. Claude wrote a production Docker Compose file and a one-command setup script: Caddy as the gateway, the web app, the stitching worker, RabbitMQ, and PostgreSQL, with data that survives restarts. My repository is private, so rather than put a GitHub token on a public server, it copied the code over SSH and deployed it. The last blocker was mine to fix: opening ports 80 and 443 in Oracle’s network firewall. Then the site was live.

I did not want to guess, so I asked Claude to load-test the live server. Simulated users ran the full flow: upload two photos, wait for the real-time notification, and download the stitched collage.

The server handled 64 people creating collages at the same moment without a single failed job: 538 collages, zero errors. Its ceiling was about 62 collages a minute—one per second. Beyond that, users queue. With 4 people creating at once, 95% of collages arrived within about five seconds; at 64, each person waited about a minute. If each active user makes a collage every couple of minutes, one CPU comfortably serves around 85 people at once, and a few hundred if they use it less often.

The test also showed what runs out first, and it is not the CPU. Each collage stores about 5 MB, mostly the PNG output, so at full speed the disk would fill in under two hours. Switching to JPEG and shortening retention fixes that, and when traffic grows, three more free CPUs are waiting. That is the value of measuring before paying: I know what to change, and when.

Oracle isn’t being charitable. Servers need applications to run—ideally ones that go viral—and the free tier is a play for loyalty. Oracle wants successful projects to stay and grow into its paid services instead of moving off the platform once they reach critical mass. It can also reclaim free instances that sit idle.

I think the bet is smart, and it points to a bigger trend. AI-generated code still needs energy to run and hardware to host it, even when far fewer people work on each project. As more people turn ideas into working software, demand for compute will keep growing, and I expect hosting and data centres to become a very profitable business.

For now, the combination works: Claude orchestrates the coding, QA, and DevOps, and Oracle’s free server keeps an idea online long enough to find out whether it deserves to grow.

#10354. Open Responses: What you need to know

Open Responses is a new and open inference standard. Initiated by OpenAI, built by the open source AI community, and backed by the Hugging Face ecosystem, Open Responses is based on the Responses API and is designed for the future of Agents. In this blog post, we’ll look at how Open Responses works and why the open source community should use Open Responses.

The era of the chatbot is long gone, and agents dominate inference workloads. Developers are shifting toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act over long-time horizons. Despite this shift, much of the ecosystem still uses the Chat Completion format, which was designed for turn-based conversations and falls short for agentic use cases. The Responses format was designed to address these limitations, but it is closed and not as widely adopted. The Chat Completion format is still the de facto standard despite the alternatives.

This mismatch between the agentic workflow requirements and entrenched interfaces motivates the need for an open inference standard. Over the coming months, we will collaborate with the community and inference providers to implement and adapt Open Responses to a shared format, practically capable of replacing chat completions.

Open Responses builds on the direction OpenAI has set with their Responses API launched in March 2025, which superseded the existing Completion and Assistants APIs with a consistent way to:

Open Responses extends and open-sources the Responses API, making it more accessible for builders and routing providers to interoperate and collaborate on shared interests.

We’ll briefly explore the core changes that impact most community members. If you want to deep dive into the specification, check out the Open Responses documentation.

Client requests to Open Responses are similar to the existing Responses API. Below we demonstrate a request to the Open Responses API using curl. We're calling a proxy endpoint that routes to Inference Providers using the Open Responses API schema.

Clients that already support the Responses API can migrate to Open Responses with relatively little effort. The main changes involve how reasoning content is exposed:

OpenAI models used to only expose summary and encrypted_content. With Open Responses, providers may expose their raw reasoning via the API. Clients migrating from providers that previously returned only summaries and encrypted content will now have the opportunity to receive and handle raw reasoning streams when supported by their chosen provider.

For Model Providers, implementing the changes for Open Responses should be straightforward if they already adhere to the Responses API specification. For Routers, there is now the opportunity to standardize on a consistent endpoint and support configuration options for customization where needed.

Over time, as Providers continue to innovate, certain features will become standardized in the base specification.

In summary, migrating to Open Responses will make the inference experience more consistent and improve quality as undocumented extensions, interpretations, and workarounds of the legacy Completions API are normalized in Open Responses.

You can see how to stream reasoning chunks below.

Here’s the difference between getting an Open Response and using OpenAI Responses for reasoning deltas:

Open Responses distinguishes between “Model Providers” — those who provide inference — and “Routers” — intermediaries who orchestrate between multiple providers.

Clients can now specify a Provider along with provider-specific API options when making requests, allowing intermediary Routers to orchestrate requests between upstream providers.

Open Responses natively supports two categories of tools: internal and external. Externally hosted tools are implemented outside the model provider’s system. For example, client side functions to be executed, or MCP servers. Internally hosted tools are within the model provider’s system. For example, OpenAI’s file search or Google Drive integration. The model calls, executes, and retrieves results entirely within the provider's infrastructure, requiring no developer intervention.

Open Responses formalizes the agentic loop which is usually made up of a repeating cycle of reasoning, tool invocation, and response generation that enables models to autonomously complete multi-step tasks.

For internally-hosted tools, the provider manages the entire loop; executing tools, returning results to the model, and streaming output. This means that multi-step workflows like "search documents, summarize findings, then draft an email" use a single request.

Clients control loop behavior via max_tool_calls to cap iterations and tool_choice to constrain which tools are invocable:

The response contains all intermediate items: tool calls, results, reasoning.

Open Responses extends and improves the Responses API, providing richer and more detailed content definitions, compatibility, and deployment options. It also provides a standard way to execute sub-agent loops during primary inference calls, opening up powerful capabilities for AI Applications. We are looking forward to working with the Open Responses team and the community at large on future development of the specification.

You can try Open Responses with Hugging Face Inference Providers today. We have an early access version available for use on Hugging Face Spaces - try it with your Client and Open Responses Compliance Tool today!

Use Open Responses with Hugging Face Inference Providers

Does this mean that the next step for local llm endpoint providers (like vLLM) is to support hosted tools?

Yes - I think we will see a lot more of this pattern especially for Agents offloading work to sub-agent Tool Loops via Open Responses.

Are you going to open source the code of the API?

I hope this doesn't normalize the obscuring of raw output.

Maybe there is a use for this. We donot need an "agent loop" insider the vendor boxes.What we definitely need is a good omni-adopted API for basic inference without anything more than general custom tool calling.

Only putting in inference paramters and that's that. I suppose that is the reason why the community stayed with the Completions API yet, right?

Agent loops are supposed to be implemented in the agent system not in the LLM vendors system.They can simply add their proprietary Agent loop thingy as an "internal" tool.

However I would highly urge the community to consider the strategic implications for further evolution of these tools. There is the danger that specific vendor based models might be highly optimized to only provide good responses on their internal tools / subagent loops. Of course they have an incentive to control the whole workflow to secure their marketshare.

Opposed to that: when everyone is using the APIs in their custom designed loop-procedure (or some from open source agent orchestration tools) the decision about what models to use is somewhat dependent on the basis of how well theses behave with external tool calling. This is rather the situation we want to be in.

Just 128MB of RAM is enough to boot Windows 11.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NTDEV, the popular developer behind the Tiny11 project, has once again pushed the limits of just how little hardware is required to run Windows 11. In a video shared on YouTube, the developer claims to have successfully booted the latest Windows 11 26H2 on a system with just 128MB of RAM. Despite severe memory constraints, the heavily stripped-down installation manages to load the Desktop and File Explorer, access the Start menu, and even run the classic Notepad app.

While it is an impressive achievement, the developer acknowledges that the system is "painfully slow," making this more of a technical experiment than a practical way to run Windows 11 on older hardware. According to Microsoft’s official requirements, Windows 11 requires at least 4GB of RAM, meaning NTDEV's latest experiment uses just 3.125% of the recommended minimum. The developer has not shared a detailed breakdown of every component removed or disabled to achieve the result, but the project builds on years of experimentation with stripped-down Windows installations.

This is not NTDEV's first attempt at pushing Windows 11 beyond its usual hardware limitations. Back in 2023, the developer managed to get the operating system running with only 176MB of RAM by extensively trimming its system components, drivers, and background services. That experiment relied on an IDE storage interface to reduce the number of drivers required, and sacrificed the standard Windows desktop environment.

Last month, the developer showcased another interesting experiment that squeezed an entire Windows 11 installation into a CD-ROM-sized ISO file. The experimental build created using the developer's upcoming Pico11 tool weighs in at 699,811,840 bytes and retains a functional Windows desktop. The stripped-down version of Windows 11 successfully boots into the desktop environment and runs basic applications such as Calculator, Settings, Notepad, and Paint. The test was conducted on a virtual machine with 4GB of allocated RAM, with the operating system using around 883MB.

Such experiments are a great way to showcase just how much of Windows can be stripped away while still retaining some of its core functionality. At the end of the day, they are primarily technical demonstrations with the intention of exploring the limits of Microsoft's operating system rather than providing practical alternatives to a standard Windows installation. Stripping away essential components, drivers, and background services comes with significant trade-offs, including reduced functionality, compatibility issues, and severely degraded performance.

#10352. Introducing Waypoint-1: Real-time interactive video diffusion from Overworld

Overworld Stream: https://overworld.stream

Waypoint-1 is Overworld’s real-time-interactive video diffusion model, controllable and prompted via text, mouse, and keyboard. You can give the model some frames, run the model, and have it create a world you can step into and interact with.

The backbone of the model is a frame-causal rectified flow transformer trained on 10,000 hours of diverse video game footage paired with control inputs and text captions. Waypoint-1 is a latent model, meaning that it is trained on compressed frames.

The standard among existing world models has become taking pre-trained video models and fine-tuning them with brief and simplified control inputs. In contrast, Waypoint-1 is trained from the get-go with a focus on interactive experiences. With other models, controls are simple: you can move and rotate the camera once every few frames, with severe latency issues. With Waypoint-1 you are not limited at all as far as controls are concerned. You can move the camera freely with the mouse, and input any key on the keyboard, and all this with zero latency. Each frame is generated with your controls as context. Additionally, the model runs fast enough to provide a seamless experience even on consumer hardware.

Waypoint-1 was pre-trained via diffusion forcing, a technique with which the model learns to denoise future frames given past frames. A causal attention mask is applied such that a token in any given frame can only attend to tokens in its own frame, or past frames, but not future frames. Each frame is noised randomly, and as such the model learns to denoise each frame separately. During inference, you can then denoise new frames one at a time, allowing you to generate a procedural stream of new frames.

While diffusion forcing presents a strong baseline, randomly noising all frames is misaligned with a frame-by-frame autoregressive rollout. This inference mismatch results in error accumulation, and noisy long rollouts. To address this problem we post-train with self forcing, a technique that trains the model to produce realistic outputs under a regime which matches inference behavior. Self-forcing via DMD has the added benefit of one-pass CFG, and few-step denoising.

WorldEngine is Overworld’s high‑performance inference library for interactive world model streaming. It provides the core tooling for building inference applications in pure Python, optimized for low latency, high throughput, extensibility, and developer simplicity. The runtime loop is designed for interactivity: it consumes context frame images, keyboard/mouse inputs, and text, and outputs image frames for real‑time streaming.

On Waypoint‑1‑Small (2.3B) running on a 5090, WorldEngine sustains ~30,000 token‑passes/sec (single denoising pass; 256 tokens per frame) and achieves 30 FPS at 4 steps or 60 FPS at 2 steps

We’d love to see what you can come up with to extend the world_engine and it should be a great event to meet like-minded founders, engineers, hackers and investors. #10351. Gemini 4 Carbon lags just behind Claude in benchmark, but wins in value

Google’s new frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, brings some welcome improvements and while it doesn’t top the charts in a new benchmark, it does provide much more bang for your buck.

SemiAnalysis, an AI research and analysis firm, recently published its new frontier-level benchmark, GDPx which includes numbers for Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon model. The leaderboard includes every major frontier model from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta and details both the score and cost for each model.

The benchmark includes 206 tasks across finance, materials science, cybersecurity, software engineering, legal, biology, and several other domains (topics).

Topping the results is Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, but Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is very close behind. The difference between the two is relatively minimal, but the cost is the biggest factor to consider here. Where Claude’s cost came out to around $51 per task, Gemini was just over $16 per task. Gemini also beat the next model on the list, GPT-6 Astra, which scored lower while costing more than both at about $54 per task.

The report notes that taking out cybersecurity, biology, and alignment domains shuffles the results. Safety guardrails in Claude and GPT models puts GPT-6 Astra at the top of the list with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 outranking Gemini 4 Carbon. SemiAnalysis says that this better aligns with their “subjective impressions” of each model.

As for Google’s existing frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, it ranks in eighth place on both lists, beating Meta’s Muse Wonder, but below Wonder Full. Argon’s costs in this particular benchmark are only slightly lower than Carbon.

Both of Google’s models score better than OpenAI and Anthropic models when focused on cybersecurity, but do fall behind Meta’s Muse models, which the benchmark found to be the best “by a meaningful margin.”

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28 and touted “significant gains,” but the public release date has not been confirmed just yet. It is “coming soon” for most customers. Google’s own benchmark, below, beat GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 in many aspects.

The reduced RAM/storage trends have been set in retail for a number of months already.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The latest Steam Survey appears to show that gamers blessed with systems packing 32GB or more RAM and 1TB or more storage are a dwindling breed. This survey is posted without comment by Valve, as usual, but appears to show a significant proportional rise in gamers using 8GB and 16GB RAM PCs, which occurs largely at the expense of the 32GB brigade. The latest stats also show a noticeable increase in storage capacity poverty in the last month. Are the symptoms of the AI industry-induced components crunch now becoming evident among the PC gaming public?

The AI-pocalypse delivered components crunch has been in the headlines for months but it is still jarring to see it impact the vast PC gaming landscape. When we’ve browsed desktop and laptop PCs for the best gaming PC deals over the past months, the trend is clear. Systems that look like they are designed for gamers or enthusiasts are now frequently fitted with just 16GB of RAM as standard, and also feature smaller storage devices that one might have expected. But to see the Steam Survey suggesting that the share of 32GB systems has now collapsed by -5.16% is startling. Only last month, 32GB was the most popular configuration among gamers according to the same survey.

RAM is probably the hardest-hit component segment of AI-driven demand so far. We maintain a RAM price tracking page at Tom’s Hardware and the current state of the market means that DIYers or upgraders need to spend about $250 for 16GB DDR5 or $450 for 32GB DDR5. Those prices change regularly, as well.

Moving onto the sudden recorded change in storage configurations in use by Steam gamers, and we see that folks with 1TB of total fixed storage space or above shrunk by 4.68%. As the categories are currently defined, this appears to show the reduction in the number of systems coming with either a 2TB and 4TB SSD as standard. That’s because the 750GB to 999GB category grew +2.36%, and Windows registers a '1TB' boot disk as a smaller (a quick check shows ours at 924GB). 250GB to 499GB total storage systems were also up a similar amount (+2.30%). Overall, it looks like systems being used for Steam gaming are increasingly fitted with these smaller capacity SSDs. Enthusiasts, gamers, and DIYers wanting to expand their storage at the best prices are advised to keep an eye on our frequently updated SSD price tracking page.

We are currently seeing some extraordinary things in the GPU market, with reports of RTX 5090 and RTX 5080 cards being removed from retail. In the Steam Survey this month the RTX 5080 is still at position 14. However, the joint most popular GPUs are the RTX 5070 and the aging RTX 3060 – both with 3.78% of the market.

We are aware that there are sometimes some strong undercurrents in the Steam Survey that cause unusual fluctuations in the figures. However, the numbers this month don’t look like they have been impacted by a Chinese user or Chinese internet café PC influx, which have previously shown odd trends (such as a rise in Windows 10 usage). Actually, the Steam Survey shows Chinese (Simplified) language users surveyed are sharply down this month, so the survey should more accurately represent the system configurations typical among gamers in the West.

#10349. Differential Transformer V2

We introduce Differential Transformer V2 (DIFF V2), an improved version of Differential Transformer (DIFF V1). This revision focuses on inference efficiency, training stability for production-level LLMs, and architectural elegance.

We conduct pretraining experiments on production-scale LLMs, including dense models and a 30A3 MoE on trillions of tokens using large learning rate of 6e-4 to 1e-3. Experimental observations:

The experiments are still running. We expect to explore in later stages of training:

After the experiments complete and we evaluate the results, we will prepare a more formal report.

(For simplicity, we omit the batch dimension and assume that both the input and output of the following flash_attn_func are three-dimensional tensors (tokens, heads, head dimension). Heads belonging to the same GQA group are arranged contiguously in the output)

Note DIFF V2 subtracts two heads that are in the same GQA group, which means they share the same key and value. This is crucial to performance. See design ablations section and Github code.

Full code at: unilm/Diff-Transformer/Diff-Transformer-V2 at master · microsoft/unilm In the script, h represents number of query heads, h_kv represents number of key-value heads, and d means head dimension. The λ\lambdaλ in DIFF V2 is projected from XXX for each token each head.

DIFF V2 doubles number of query heads while maintaining number of key value heads, and the extra dimension is reduced back to h*d after the differential operation so the WOW_OWO​ projection remains the same as baseline Transformer.

DIFF V2 introduces additional query heads compared to the baseline Transformer, but does not increase the number of key-value (KV) heads. Since LLM decoding is typically memory-bound, this design allows DIFF V2 to achieve decoding speeds on par with standard Transformer. Besides, since head dimension is aligned between query, key and value, there is no need for custom attention kernels for DIFF V2. In contrast, DIFF V1 can be slower during decoding because the value cache must be loaded twice, and a custom attention kernel is needed. DIFF V2 can also increase the arithmetic intensity of the attention module during decoding.

During pretraining, when using cutting-edge FlashAttention kernels on H-series and B-series GPUs, the throughput reduction introduced by DIFF V2 is negligible. For long-sequence prefilling, we recommend combining DIFF V2 with techniques such as YOCO (also used in Gemma 3n), which already reduces prefilling complexity to linear time with respect to sequence length.

An alternative perspective is to compare DIFF V2 with a Transformer that has the same query dimension 2h*d. Under this comparison, both models exhibit same attention kernel speed, while DIFF V2 has less parameters and flops in output projection.

In the standard Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA), let Q,K,V∈Rn×dQ, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}Q,K,V∈Rn×d be the queries, keys, and values. The context vector CCC is defined as:

Where A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is the attention weight matrix. Let's focus on a single row of CCC, denoted as ci\mathbf{c}_ici​, which is a weighted sum of value vectors vj\mathbf{v}_jvj​:

ci=∑j=1naijvj \mathbf{c}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} \mathbf{v}_j ci​=j=1∑n​aij​vj​

We define the Context RMS (Root Mean Square) to represent the magnitude of this output:

RMS(ci)=1d∥ci∥2 \text{RMS}(\mathbf{c}_i) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{d} \|\mathbf{c}_i\|^2} RMS(ci​)=d1​∥ci​∥2​

The weights aija_{ij}aij​ are non-negative and sum to 1 ( ∑j=1naij=1\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} = 1∑j=1n​aij​=1 ). Assume the value vectors vj\mathbf{v}_jvj​ are uncorrelated and have an RMS of 1, the Context RMS is strictly bounded in range [1n,1)[\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}},1)[n​1​,1) however the attention distribution changes:

In DIFF V1 we add a per-head RMSNorm on context vectors:

c^i=ciRMS(ci) \mathbf{\hat{c}}_i = \frac{\mathbf{c}_i}{\text{RMS}(\mathbf{c}_i)} c^i​=RMS(ci​)ci​​

If the model learns a uniform attention distribution in a head, the Context RMS is approximately 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n​. To normalize this back to 111, RMSNorm must multiply the vector by a scale of n\sqrt{n}n​. For n=8192n = 8192n=8192, n≈90.5\sqrt{n} \approx 90.5n​≈90.5. This means the RMSNorm layer applies a 100x magnification to the output. In large-scale pretraining, we find this leads to massive gradients and numerical instability.

A typical phenomenon is that when DIFF V1 is pre-trained at a large learning rate, the gradient norm experiences a larger increase compared to Transformer in the later stages, along with higher variance. In DIFF V2, after removing the per-head RMSNorm, the gradient norm scale becomes comparable to that of Transformer, and the gradient norm spike is reduced (will be discussed further below).

We adopted the per-head RMSNorm design in DIFF V1 primarily because of the doubled value head dimension and the globally shared λ\lambdaλ across all tokens. Given the modifications made to these two aspects in DIFF V2, we found that removing RMSNorm is now safe.

We demonstrate DIFF V2 can overcome the constraint of Softmax mentioned above. It can also help eliminate attention sinks.

We expect to explore in later stages of training:

In theory, a standard Transformer with 2h2h2h attention heads can learn the differential operation by learning WO2i=−WO2i+1,i=0,1,…,h−1W_O^{2i}=-W_O^{2i+1}, i=0,1,\ldots,h-1WO2i​=−WO2i+1​,i=0,1,…,h−1, where WOiW_O^{i}WOi​ denotes the output projection of head iii, and head 2i2i2i and 2i+12i+12i+1 belong to the same GQA group.

Assumption 1. In practice, such a solution is difficult to learn through optimization, as it requires two sets of parameters to converge to exact negatives of each other.

Assumption 2. The differential operation can be learned by the model and the model chooses to learn it in the training. Then explicitly constructing it before the output projection as in DIFF V2 can save half of the WOW_OWO​ parameters. The number of saved parameters is also non-trivial. Under the current GQA setting, the parameters in the attention module are dominated by WQW_QWQ​ and WOW_OWO​; Therefore, approximately 25% of the attention-module parameters can be saved. The saved parameter budget can then be reallocated to other parts of the model.

Even if DIFF V2, after reallocating parameters, does not achieve a lower loss than the baseline but merely matches it, the method is still worthwhile if it provides additional benefits such as improved training stability, better control of outliers, or higher training efficiency. This is analogous to GQA, which matches the loss of MHA while reducing KV-cache as an additional benefit. So the key question becomes empirical performance.

(For simplicity, we omit the batch dimension and assume that both the input and output of the following flash_attn_func are three-dimensional tensors (tokens, heads, head dimension). Heads belonging to the same GQA group are arranged contiguously in the output)

In our large learning rate setting, the ablation 1 setting exhibits obvious training instability (much more loss and gradient spikes) and higher loss comparing to DIFF V2. The value should be shared in the two subtraction heads to construct differential operation, as discussed in DIFF V1 paper.

Both ablation 2 and ablation 3 lead to higher language modeling loss than DIFF V2. Ablation 2 maintains training stability similar to DIFF V2, whereas ablation 3 is less stable (still more stable than ablation 1).

Ablation 4 also has higher training loss comparing to DIFF V2.

This is a fascinating and thorough update on the Differential Transformer architecture. The transition from DIFF V1 to V2 addresses some critical practical hurdles in a very elegant way.

The key design choice of doubling query heads within shared GQA groups is clever. It successfully decouples the innovative "differential" attention operation from the need for custom kernels, making it a much more viable drop-in replacement for standard attention. The analysis of how this design overcomes the softmax magnitude constraint and helps eliminate attention sinks is particularly convincing.

The reported early results—lower loss, reduced gradient spikes, and better control of activation outliers, especially at large learning rates—are highly promising. It suggests DIFF V2 isn't just a parameter-saving trick but may offer fundamental improvements in training dynamics and stability.

I have a couple of questions out of curiosity:

Long-Context Performance: You mention exploring "context rot" alleviation in later stages. Given the modified attention output dynamics, do you have any early hypotheses on whether DIFF V2 might inherently improve performance on very long sequences compared to a baseline Transformer with similar parameter budgets?

Broader Application: The principle seems powerful yet simple. Beyond the dense and MoE models tested here, do you see potential for applying this differential attention mechanism in other architectures, like state-space models or multimodal transformers?

#10348. Building a Human Review Pipeline for AI Search: A Practical Developer’s Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An AI search feature can return valid JSON, render correctly, and still give an unhelpful answer.

Imagine a documentation assistant answering a question about an API's current authentication requirements. It retrieves an outdated page, summarizes it fluently, and displays a citation. Every technical component appears to work, but the user receives instructions that no longer apply.

Automated checks are valuable, yet they cannot replace a clearly defined judgment about whether an answer solves the user's problem.

This guide builds a human-review workflow for a hypothetical API documentation assistant. You will define a review rubric, validate submissions with Python, measure reviewer disagreement, and turn accepted judgments into regression cases. The Python examples use Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn; they do not require a model-provider API key.

Start by identifying the failure you want to detect.

A documentation assistant usually has several stages: receive a question, retrieve relevant documents, generate an answer, and present that answer with supporting material.

Do not collapse these into a single “good answer” rating. A low score without a reason tells the team little about what to fix.

SitePoint’s introduction to retrieval-augmented generation provides background on how retrieval and generation fit together.

Preserve the exact question, answer revision, retrieved passages, document versions, and retrieval timestamp for each run. Store a snapshot manifest with stable passage IDs, source URLs, and content hashes. Reviewers should see the material supplied to that run, not today’s edited page. Keep the model and prompt configuration with the run so a later review can be traced to the behavior it evaluated.

A useful rubric defines observable criteria and separates evidence support from task completion and source suitability. Give each review the same user task and expected API version. Otherwise, reviewers may judge different questions while appearing to disagree about one answer.

For an answer about API authentication, use separate labels such as:

Supported: every material factual claim is backed by the supplied evidence.

Partially supported: some material claims lack support, while others are grounded.

Unsupported: the answer's central instruction lacks support or contradicts the evidence.

Cannot assess: the necessary evidence is missing, unreadable, or inaccessible.

Define task completion independently as complete, incomplete, or cannot assess. For source suitability, use suitable, outdated, or cannot assess. An answer can faithfully summarize an obsolete page while failing the request for current instructions.

Consider a fictional API migration: version 2 accepts X-API-Key, while version 3 requires Authorization: Bearer . If the supplied evidence contains only the version 2 page, an answer repeating X-API-Key can be supported by its evidence but still use an outdated source. If the evidence explicitly requires Bearer and the answer invents X-API-Key, label the answer unsupported. These are different engineering failures.

Also establish what reviewers should do when the source is outdated. They may correctly conclude that an answer reflects its evidence while separately flagging that evidence as unsuitable for the user's current task.

Start with a calibration batch covering clear successes, unsupported claims, missing evidence, and version mismatches. Have two reviewers label the same items independently, then compare their reasons. Revise ambiguous definitions before increasing volume; the batch is for improving the rubric, not estimating production quality.

Keep a rubric version on every review. Labels produced under different definitions should not be mixed without checking comparability.

A spreadsheet can help during exploration, but an engineering pipeline needs a stable record format.

Pydantic can validate a review record before it enters the dataset. Install Pydantic 2 and scikit-learn in your project environment, then use this model:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError

model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)

answer_revision: str = Field(min_length=1)

completion: Literal["complete", "incomplete", "cannot_assess"]

source_fit: Literal["suitable", "outdated", "cannot_assess"]

rationale: str = Field(min_length=20, max_length=2000)

Strict mode limits type coercion, and extra="forbid" rejects unexpected fields. The model checks shape and allowed values; it cannot establish that a judgment is correct. A minimum rationale length does not guarantee a useful explanation. The snapshot ID references a manifest, which can also record that retrieval produced no usable passages.

On the server, resolve the item, answer revision, snapshot, and passage IDs against the stored run. Reject IDs that do not belong together. Obtain the reviewer identity from the authenticated session rather than trusting a submitted reviewer_id. Store a server-generated submission time and preserve review revisions instead of silently overwriting earlier judgments.

Run this after the model definition. It accepts one fictional review and rejects both an unknown label and an extra field:

"rationale": "The answer invents X-API-Key; p1 requires Bearer.",

raise AssertionError("Invalid review was accepted")

The expected error types are literal_error and extra_forbidden. Add separate integration tests for mismatched evidence IDs, unauthorized submissions, and retries. Use a database uniqueness rule or an idempotency key so a repeated request does not create a second independent review.

More reviews do not automatically produce better evidence. If a task is ambiguous, scaling it can simply reproduce the ambiguity.

The workflow needs clear eligibility requirements, examples, escalation routes, and acceptance criteria. Reviewers assessing API behavior may need domain knowledge that general writing fluency does not provide.

If you work with an external AI-data contributor service such as Acquirox, define the task contract before assigning work: required expertise, permitted source material, output fields, and escalation rules. Keep ownership of the rubric, evaluation set, and acceptance decisions within the product team. Contributor capacity alone does not establish expertise in the API being reviewed.

Pilot the actual task in the review interface. Track drafts, submitted reviews, items needing adjudication, and final decisions as distinct workflow states. Reviewer judgments should remain immutable once submitted; corrections should create a new revision with a reason. Keep adjudication separate from the original labels.

For data involving users or contributors, document permitted uses, access boundaries, and retention. Remove credentials and unnecessary personal information from review material. An internal support transcript should not become a broadly accessible annotation task by accident.

Distinguish annotation from usability research. A skilled reviewer can judge whether an answer is supported, but that does not prove a first-time user can understand the interface.

SitePoint’s guide to choosing usability tests and participants offers related guidance on matching participants and methods to the question being investigated.

The review interface shapes the data it collects.

Label Studio is an option for configurable labeling interfaces and data import/export. If you use it, map exported annotations into the Review schema through an adapter; do not assume its export structure matches your application contract. A custom interface may be appropriate when reviewers need API-version navigation or passage-level citations.

The original question and relevant user context.

The evidence snapshot supplied to the model.

Separate controls for support and task completion.

A rationale field and an explicit “cannot assess” option.

Display stable passage IDs beside the evidence and let reviewers attach those IDs to their rationale. Show the source version and retrieval time near each passage. Render retrieved content as untrusted text or sanitized markup, and never treat instructions embedded in a source document as reviewer instructions. Avoid loading executable third-party content inside the review panel.

Avoid showing a preferred model name or a previous reviewer's verdict before an independent judgment. For pairwise comparisons, randomize answer order and include appropriate tie or neither-acceptable outcomes.

Design for keyboard use, visible focus, readable text, and explicit selection states. Keep evidence and the answer accessible without requiring excessive horizontal scrolling.

Start all judgment controls unselected and validate them on submission. Use labeled radio groups, an accessible error summary, and visible saving/submission status. A failed save should preserve the draft. Disable duplicate submissions in the UI, but enforce duplicate handling on the server as well.

Practical check: observe a reviewer completing several borderline examples. Record where they pause, misinterpret a label, or cannot find the necessary source material.

When two reviewers disagree, investigate before reducing their decisions to a majority vote.

Different assumptions about the user's expertise.

A genuine error by one or both reviewers.

Preserve independent labels and store the adjudicated result separately. This allows the team to study ambiguity instead of erasing it.

For two reviewers applying categorical labels to the same items, scikit-learn provides Cohen's kappa:

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score

("q1", "a1", "s1", "auth-v1"): "supported",

("q2", "a1", "s2", "auth-v1"): "unsupported",

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "supported",

("q4", "a1", "s4", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

("q3", "a1", "s3", "auth-v1"): "partially_supported"

raise ValueError("Review sets must contain identical items")

raw_agreement = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(left, right)) / len(keys)

print(f"Raw agreement: {raw_agreement:.2f}")

print(f"Kappa: {cohen_kappa_score(left, right):.2f}")

This toy example prints raw agreement of 0.75 and kappa of about 0.64. Four items are not enough to assess a review program. In production, check for duplicate reviews before building dictionaries, use one rubric version per comparison, report unmatched items, and align all records by item, answer revision, and evidence snapshot.

Kappa measures agreement beyond chance under its assumptions, not correctness. Inspect raw agreement, label frequencies, and the disagreement table alongside it. A single-category batch can make kappa undefined; report that limitation rather than substituting a reassuring score. Treat cannot_assess explicitly and report its frequency instead of silently excluding difficult cases.

If both reviewers apply the same flawed rubric consistently, agreement can be high while the evaluation remains unhelpful.

Once difficult cases are adjudicated, turn them into regression cases with explicit acceptance criteria. For the fictional authentication task: use version 3 evidence, cite the passage requiring Bearer, and do not invent a header. If version 3 evidence is missing, an acceptable response should explain the gap rather than provide confident instructions.

Expected behavior or acceptance criteria.

DVC can track larger datasets alongside Git. In an existing Git repository with DVC initialized and data/reviewed-auth.jsonl present, a minimal versioning step is:

git add data/reviewed-auth.jsonl.dvc data/.gitignore

git commit -m "Version authentication review cases"

This commits metadata, not the dataset bytes. Configure an access-controlled DVC remote and push the data before expecting another machine or CI runner to retrieve it. Keep credentials and sensitive review material out of public repositories.

Keep development examples separate from held-out evaluation cases. If developers repeatedly tune prompts against the same questions, those questions become less useful as evidence of generalization.

Split related examples together where appropriate. Near-duplicate questions from one support conversation should not be scattered across development and evaluation sets.

Use two evaluation passes. First, hold the evidence snapshot fixed to compare answer-generation changes. Then test retrieval against the intended document versions to detect stale or irrelevant sources. Record per-item outcomes and report failures by category; an overall improvement can hide a regression in version-specific or multilingual questions.

SitePoint’s article on testing nondeterministic AI behavior provides further context for repeatable evaluation workflows.

A correct answer can still fail in the interface.

Users may overlook a caveat, misunderstand whether an operation has been performed, or miss that the evidence applies to an older API version.

Pair answer review with practical usability tasks:

Find the authentication requirements for version 3 and identify the source that supports them.

Observe whether users complete the task and whether their confidence matches the available evidence.

SitePoint’s overview of user research methods helps distinguish task observation from preference surveys.

Turn interface failures into browser tests: a citation opens the expected document version, its passage ID matches the displayed evidence, missing evidence offers a recovery action, and a failed review submission preserves the draft. Verify that reviewers cannot access unassigned restricted items by changing an ID in the URL. These checks complement human judgments; they do not replace them.

Do not use a fluent response as a substitute for a clear interaction. The interface should distinguish retrieved information, generated interpretation, and actions the application has actually completed.

Start with one authentication task, a versioned rubric, and a small calibration batch. Use Pydantic for ingestion checks, Label Studio or a custom interface for review, scikit-learn for agreement analysis, and Git/DVC for dataset provenance. Add each tool only when it solves a concrete workflow need.

At release time, run deterministic checks for schema, evidence references, permissions, and interface behavior. Compare candidate answers against adjudicated acceptance criteria and send new ambiguous failures back for review. Record the dataset revision and configurations with the results so another developer can reproduce the comparison.

The purpose of human review is to produce evidence the team can act on. A smaller collection of well-defined, traceable judgments is often more useful than a large pile of ratings whose meaning nobody can explain.

Is it smuggling if it's technically legal?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A memory smuggler has detailed how he gets export-controlled HBM chips from South Korea into China using a loophole. According to The Information, the smuggler owns a chip design firm that build cheap, low-performing processors that fall under the U.S. and South Korea’s export controls. They are then paired with expensive HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, that, on their own, are banned for export to China. But because export control rules only look at the performance of the server processor and not at the other components attached to it, this allows the HBM chips attached inside them to slip under the radar and make their way into China.

It’s not a risk-free operation, though. Once the mediocre processors with high-end memory chips land in Hong Kong and are smuggled across the border into Shenzhen in the luggage of commuters that cross between the two regions daily, they end up in workshops where technicians heat up the boards to soften the solder, gingerly lift the crucial memory chips, and discard the rest of the components. Despite having a high failure rate, the high price of HBM chips makes the procedure quite lucrative.

A Shenzhen-based chip broker has been making big money matching up suppliers such as the smuggler and companies that are desperate for HBM. “A year ago, a single HBM3E unit changed hands in China for several hundred dollars,” he tells the publication. “Today it’s about $4,000.” With an AI chip requiring six to eight high-end memory chips, that means the broker is raking in $24,000 to $32,000 for every AI GPU.

Chinese AI labs face this exact memory chip bottleneck when acquiring AI GPUs. While Chinese memory manufacturer CXMT has already begun risk production of HBM3E and is expected to mass produce them by the end of this year, it’s still reportedly suffering from low yield, which makes their chips expensive to produce and procure. We see this with Huawei’s Ascend 950DT, its current top-of-the-line processor that goes for about $37,000 — it offers similar pricing to Nvidia’s B200 AI GPU but only delivers half the performance of the previous-generation H100.

Huawei has reportedly said that its next-generation flagship AI processor, the 960DT, would deliver a similar performance as the H100. However, since the company cannot purchase HBM from Samsung and SK hynix, and Chinese memory manufacturers do not have the capacity to supply all its chip demands, Huawei told customers that they have to find the HBM that these servers need themselves. This would further fuel the demand for these chips, increase the price and make it more lucrative for smugglers to set up similar operations.

But given that this method of moving HBM chips into China is becoming more popular, the smuggler fears that South Korean and U.S. authorities would clamp down on their operations soon. Washington has been going down hard on activities like this, and we’ve seen high-profile arrests including some Super Micro executives and the CEO of a California-based tech company. Other countries like Taiwan and Malaysia have been ramping up their anti-smuggling activities, too, so it’s probably just a matter of time before Seoul follows suit.
