#10313. Android gaming is having a renaissance

Good morning! Today I’m mourning the loss of Patrick Stewart by rewatching First Contact, my favorite Trek movie; beginning a marathon listen of at least one great Star Trek podcast; and replaying Elite Force and Armada, both wonderful Trek games released in 2000.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

I’m starting this edition of Inbox a bit later than I’d like, but for a good reason: I got swept up by the subject I was researching. See, I wanted to write about the seeming renaissance of gaming on Android, which has always had clear advantages and disadvantages compared to iOS. On the plus side, its openness bred experimentation and a healthy indie gaming scene, along with a thriving emulation ecosystem born of its ability to sideload apps and gain access to Android’s underlying file system. On the downside, its device and OS version fragmentation has kept some developers from attempting challenging console and PC ports, and led others to abandon their titles to bugs and time.

But thanks to a confluence of factors, as well as form factors, Android gaming is in a very good place right now. Despite Google’s continued ambivalence towards paid and premium games, the platform has received official ports of console hits like Dredge and Sifu, with others like Replaced, Absolum, and Dispatch coming soon. (One could argue things have been good for a while with Stardew Valley, Dead Cells, Balatro, Slay the Spire, and Vampire Crawlers available already, but I digress.)

Most of these games are embracing a try-before-you-buy model to avoid the upfront cost that so many mobile users resist, while others, like Dispatch, are getting a mobile optimization that reorients the experience for a portrait display.

And while traditional emulation has existed since Android was young, recent months have seen considerable improvement in breadth and performance, aided by AI coding tools and a community that wants to play its library of Steam, Windows, and Switch games on phones. This rabbit hole is extensive and varied: WinNative combines work from Winlator Bionic and Pluvia to run Windows games on Android and connect PC storefront libraries. DroidDeck aims for a SteamOS-like experience, putting Steam’s Big Picture interface on supported Android hardware with Windows games running through ARM64 Proton, which debuted recently with the Steam Frame.

It’s via DroidDeck that I whiled away a couple of glorious hours on my Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing Lumines Arise, a game perfectly suited to the pick-up-and-play nature of smartphones (though it’s best with a controller). The latest Qualcomm chips have long outpaced the mobile games they’ve been asked to power, but few knew just how well they’d run demanding PC and console titles, even through compatibility layers like Proton.

Similarly, an Android branch of the increasingly popular nxnative, which compiles Switch and Switch 2 games for iOS and macOS, has been making it easy to play games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Metroid Dread at 60fps on many recent Qualcomm-powered devices. There’s even a Switch 2 version in the works for Android.

The big question is whether all of this works well: will people spend more time arguing with the software than playing the games themselves? And on the legal side of the business, will publishers find success selling discounted versions of AAA titles on Android now that the translation tools are better and the device compatibility much broader?

If there’s one thing I’ve learned covering Android for nearly 20 years, it’s that the community always finds a way.

ICYMI: Ben’s Weekender essay is all about how Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly.

The strangest thing I’ve seen recently is the rumor that Elon Musk wants to launch a Starlink-branded terrestrial wireless carrier in the US. Now we know how he plans to do it: by purchasing Boost Mobile from EchoStar and leveraging its contracts with AT&T and T-Mobile along with new low- and mid-band spectrum Starlink recently acquired. That infrastructure, combined with Starlink’s existing array of LEO satellites, could make for a compelling advantage over the incumbents: namely, that dead spots practically won’t exist anymore.

But as we’ve learned from countless examples over the years, running a low-margin, high-churn postpaid wireless business is not for the faint of heart, and I’m not sure why Musk has decided that now is the right time to do it.

Five years on, is the Pixel 6 series really the disaster that we remember it being? The answer, according to Damien Wilde, is a bit more nuanced.

The Pixel 6 and Pixel 6 Pro were fundamentally flawed pioneers for Google. They were the firm’s most ambitious hardware undertaking to date, and simultaneously one of the most frustrating phone series to live with during their initial launch window and beyond. If the Pixel 5 was a safe play ahead of this big pitch, the Pixel 6 was a risky dive into deep waters. It stumbled badly. Yet without those painful growing pains, the more polished, confident, and reliable Pixel devices we enjoy today simply would not exist.

Finally, networked supermarket freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and Luxembourg were hacked over the weekend, sending temperatures up to a reported 50 degrees Celsius, and all the food inside them straight into the trash.

According to Reuters, “The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.”

Apple is about to feel the squeeze from rising memory prices, with the cost of RAM climbing just as the company heads into its busiest shopping season. According to Reuters, Apple expects to pay more for memory in the December quarter, with the CEO, John Ternus, describing the current price increases as “unprecedented. The company has so far managed to soften the blow by using memory bought at lower prices, cutting costs elsewhere and raising prices on some products. However, it is reported that its manufacturing bill has climbed by $33 billion in just a few months.

But that cushion is getting thinner, and Apple expects memory purchases to become even more expensive into 2027. “What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset.” Ternus said during Apple’s November 2 earnings call.

Memory is used across Apple's hardware lineup, so sustained price increases could affect manufacturing cost for several product categories—although Apple has not announced another round of price increases. Absorbing higher components could, however, indefinitely become difficult. Dave Nicholson, Chief Research Officer at the Futurum Group, also identified memory prices as a growing pressure point for Apple's margins and hardware pricing through the holiday season and into 2027. According to him, Apple is in a different position from companies pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into AI data center infrastructure. The impact of higher component costs is easier to quantify than the eventual returns on massive AI capital expenditure, he said.

The next pressure point for @Apple may not be AI CapEx, but the rising cost of memory across its hardware portfolio. @TheFuturumGroup Chief Research Officer @DaveN007 explained that higher memory prices could put more pressure on Apple’s margins and pricing through the holiday season and into 2027. Even with demand holding up, the question is how much of those higher costs consumers will absorb. Dave also sees Apple in a stronger position than companies committing hundreds of billions to data center infrastructure, because the impact of higher component costs is easier to quantify than the long-term returns on massive AI CapEx. ▶️ Watch Dave’s analysis of Apple’s margin outlook, memory costs, and why its AI infrastructure strategy could give the company more flexibility. #Apple #AI #Semiconductors #FuturumNovember 3, 2026

And the warnings from Apple's suppliers suggest that the cost pressure is unlikely to ease quickly. Last month, Samsung, a major supplier of RAM(DRAM), NAND flash storage and OLED displays for Apple, said that memory demand would far exceed supply as AI infrastructure continues to expand. Its memory division also reported a quarter-on-quarter increase in DRAM average prices during the third quarter, while NAND prices rose by high-teen percentages. Senior executive vice president of its memory business warned the supply crunch could extend to 2028 and beyond. Elsewhere, SK Hynix delivered a similar warning, saying it had secured long-term agreements covering more than Half of its production capacity for2027 and 2028. Micron, the third major supplier for Apple aside from Samsung and SK Hynix, is also benefiting from the surging demand for memory. Its latest published outlook warns that supply shortages in memory and storage could take “considerable time” to improve.

We have previously reported several signs of the pressure now confronting Apple. In January, the company was already scrambling to secure memory supplies amid strong demand, with then CEO Tim Cook warning that rising prices could have a greater impact on earnings. By June, rising component expenses had translated into higher retail prices. Apple increased prices across several Mac and iPad models, including a $400 increase to the starting price of the MacBook Pro, due to the RAM crisis. In July, Cook described the memory market as a “hundred-year-flood” and said Apple expected to pay more for memory in the September quarter. The company had also increased its inventory to $11.09 billion as it built a buffer against supply and price pressures.

#10311. How to Test AI-Generated Content Before It Reaches Your Users

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most teams now ship something an AI helped write: help-center articles, product descriptions, release notes, even code comments. The draft appears in seconds, and that speed is the trap. Nobody tests it the way they would test a new feature, so mistakes slip through that a quick review would have caught.

This guide is about the other side of AI testing. Instead of using AI to test your software, you test what AI hands you. Here is a simple routine that fits into a normal publishing or release process.

AI writing sounds confident whether or not it is right. A model can invent a statistic (researchers call this hallucination and have documented it across many text-generation systems), quote a feature your product does not have, or describe a setting that was renamed two releases ago. The sentence reads smoothly, so the error hides in plain sight.

Traditional QA does not cover this. A unit test tells you the page loads. It says nothing about whether the claim on the page is true. That gap is where most AI-related incidents begin.

1. Define what "good" means before you generate anything. Write down the audience, the claims you are willing to make and the sources you trust. A short brief makes the output easier to judge, because you are comparing it with something concrete.

2. Check every factual claim. Highlight each number, name and statement of fact, then verify it against a primary source. Google's own guidance on generative AI content tells publishers to fact-check AI output, including titles, descriptions and alt text, before publishing. If you cannot confirm a claim in a minute or two, cut it or rewrite it as something you can support.

3. Test the instructions. For tutorials and how-to content, follow the steps exactly as written on a clean machine or account. Commands that fail and menus that no longer exist show up immediately this way.

4. Review the voice. Replace vague phrases with specifics from your own experience: a real customer question, a real error message, a real number from your analytics. This is also what separates useful content from filler.

5. Keep a human owner. Every piece should have a named person who approved it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework makes the same point at organization level: people stay accountable for how AI is used and evaluated. If something goes wrong later, you know who to ask and where to fix it.

Some teams also run drafts through an AI detector. That can be useful as a prompt for a closer look, for example when freelancers or vendors deliver work and you want to know how much of it was machine-generated. A high score is a reason to read more carefully. It is not proof of anything, and it should never decide an outcome on its own, because detectors make mistakes in both directions. A Stanford study found that GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, and short texts are easy to misjudge too. If you want a quick second opinion on a draft, a tool like Tester AI can give you a starting point for that conversation.

Review works best when it is not optional. A few small habits make it stick.

Treating the first draft as finished. It is a starting point. Plan time for review the same way you plan time for writing.

Reviewing for grammar only. Clean sentences are not evidence of correct content. Check meaning first and polish second.

Letting the tool grade its own work. Asking the same model to confirm its answer rarely catches real errors. Use a source or a person.

Skipping legal and brand review. Generated text can echo existing material or make promises your company cannot keep. Anything customer-facing deserves a second pair of eyes.

AI can save hours of drafting, but speed only helps if the result is trustworthy. Treat generated content like code from a new contributor: useful, often good, and always reviewed before it goes live. A short routine of defining quality, verifying facts, testing instructions and keeping a human owner will catch most problems before your users do.

Do I need to test AI-generated content if a human edits it? Yes. Editing for style does not confirm that the facts are correct. Verify claims separately from polishing the wording.

How long should a review take? For a typical article, expect roughly the time it takes to read it twice plus a few minutes per factual claim. Reviews are faster when the brief and sources are prepared in advance.

Can an AI detector prove that text was written by a machine? No. Detectors estimate likelihood, and they can be wrong. Use the result as a signal for human review, never as the final decision.

What should I check first? Start with numbers, names, dates and anything a customer could act on, such as prices, steps or legal statements. Those carry the highest risk if they are wrong.

#10309. Training Design for Text-to-Image Models: Lessons from Ablations

Welcome back! This is the second part of our series on training efficient text-to-image models from scratch.

In the first post of this series, we introduced our goal: training a competitive text-to-image foundation model entirely from scratch, in the open, and at scale. We focused primarily on architectural choices and motivated the core design decisions behind our model PRX. We also released an early, small (1.2B parameters) version of the model as a preview of what we are building (go try it if you haven't already 😉).

In this post, we shift our focus from architecture to training. The goal is to document what actually moved the needle for us when trying to make models train faster, converge more reliably, and learn better representations. The field is moving quickly and the list of “training tricks” keeps growing, so rather than attempting an exhaustive survey, we structured this as an experimental logbook: we reproduce (or adapt) a set of recent ideas, implement them in a consistent setup, and report how they affect optimization and convergence in practice. Finally, we do not only report these techniques in isolation; we also explore which ones remain useful when combined.

In the next post, we will publish the full training recipe as code, including the experiments in this post. We will also run and report on a public "speedrun" where we put the best pieces together into a single configuration and stress-test it end-to-end. This exercise will serve both as a stress test of our current training pipeline and as a concrete demonstration of how far careful training design can go under tight constraints. If you haven’t already, we invite you to join our Discord to continue the discussion. A significant part of this project has been shaped by exchanges with community members, and we place a high value on external feedback, ablations, and alternative interpretations of the results.

Before introducing any training-efficiency techniques, we first establish a clean reference run. This baseline is intentionally simple. It uses standard components, avoids auxiliary objectives, and does not rely on architectural shortcuts or tricks to save compute resources. Its role is to serve as a stable point of comparison for all subsequent experiments.Concretely, this is a pure Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2022) training setup (as introduced in Part 1) with no extra objectives and no architectural speed hacks. We will use the small PRX-1.2B model we presented in the first post of this series (single stream architecture with global attention for the image tokens and text tokens) as our baseline and train it in Flux VAE latent space, keeping the configuration fixed across all comparisons unless stated otherwise.

The baseline training setup is as follows:

This baseline configuration provides a transparent and reproducible anchor. It allows us to attribute observed improvements and regressions to specific training interventions, rather than to shifting hyperparameters or hidden setup changes. Throughout the remainder of this post, every technique is evaluated against this reference with a single guiding question in mind:

Does this modification improve convergence or training efficiency relative to the baseline?

Examples of baseline model generations after 100K training steps.

To keep this post grounded, we rely on a small set of metrics to monitor checkpoints over time. None of them is a perfect proxy for perceived image quality, but together they provide a practical scoreboard while we iterate.

Fréchet Inception Distance (FID): (Heusel et al., 2017) Measures how close the distributions of generated and real images are, using Inception-v3 feature statistics (mean and covariance). Lower values typically correlate with higher sample fidelity.

CLIP Maximum Mean Discrepancy (CMMD): (Jayasumana et al., 2024) Measures the distance between real and generated image distributions using CLIP image embeddings and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). Unlike FID, CMMD does not assume Gaussian feature distributions and can be more sample-efficient; in practice it often tracks perceptual quality better than FID, though it is still an imperfect proxy.

DINOv2 Maximum Mean Discrepancy (DINO-MMD): Same MMD-based distance as CMMD, but computed on DINOv2 (Oquab et al. 2023) image embeddings instead of CLIP. This provides a complementary view of distribution shift under a self-supervised vision backbone.

Network throughput: Average number of samples processed per second (samples/s), as a measure of end-to-end training efficiency.

With the scoreboard defined, we can now dive into the methods we explored, grouped into four buckets: Representation Alignment, Training Objectives, Token Routing and Sparsification, and Data.

Diffusion and flow models are typically trained with a single objective: predict a noise-like target (or vector field) from a corrupted input. Early in training, that one objective is doing two jobs at once: it must build a useful internal representation and learn to denoise on top of it. Representation alignment makes this explicit by keeping the denoising objective and adding an auxiliary loss that directly supervises intermediate features using a strong, frozen vision encoder. This tends to speed up early learning and bring the model’s features closer to those of modern self-supervised encoders. As a result, you often need less compute to hit the same quality.

A useful way to view it is to decompose the denoiser into an implicit encoder that produces intermediate hidden states, and a decoder that maps those states to the denoising target. The claim is that representation learning is the bottleneck: diffusion and flow transformers do learn discriminative features, but they lag behind foundation vision encoders when training is compute-limited. Therefore, borrowing a powerful representation space can make the denoising problem easier.

REPA adds a representation matching term on top of the base flow-matching objective.Let x0∼pdatax_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}x0​∼pdata​ be a clean sample and x1∼ppriorx_1 \sim p_{\text{prior}}x1​∼pprior​ be the noise sample. The model is trained on an interpolated state xtx_txt​ (for t∈[0,1]t \in [0,1]t∈[0,1]) and predicts a vector field vθ(xt,t)v_\theta(x_t, t)vθ​(xt​,t). In REPA, a pretrained vision encoder fff processes the clean sample x0x_0x0​ to produce patch embeddings y0=f(x0)∈RN×Dy_0 = f(x_0) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}y0​=f(x0​)∈RN×D, where NNN is the number of patch tokens and DDD is the teacher embedding dimension. In parallel, the denoiser processes xtx_txt​ and produces intermediate hidden tokens hth_tht​ (one token per patch). A small projection head hϕh_\phihϕ​ maps these student hidden tokens into the teacher embedding space, and an auxiliary loss maximizes patch-wise similarity between corresponding teacher and student tokens: LREPA(θ,ϕ)=−Ex0,x1,t[1N∑n=1Nsim(y0,[n], hϕ(ht,[n]))] \mathcal{L}_{\text{REPA}}(\theta,\phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{x_0,x_1,t}\Big[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \text{sim}\big(y_{0,[n]},\, h_\phi(h_{t,[n]})\big)\Big] LREPA​(θ,ϕ)=−Ex0​,x1​,t​[N1​n=1∑N​sim(y0,[n]​,hϕ​(ht,[n]​))] Here n∈{1,…,N}n \in \{1,\dots,N\}n∈{1,…,N} indexes patch tokens, y0,[n]y_{0,[n]}y0,[n]​ is the teacher embedding for patch nnn, ht,[n]h_{t,[n]}ht,[n]​ is the corresponding student hidden token at time ttt, and sim(⋅,⋅)\text{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)sim(⋅,⋅) is typically cosine similarity.

This term is combined with the main flow-matching loss:

L=LFM+λ LREPA \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} + \lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{REPA}} L=LFM​+λLREPA​

with λ\lambdaλ controlling the trade-off.

In practice, the student is trained to produce noise-robust, data-consistent patch representations from xtx_txt​, so later layers can focus on predicting the vector field and generating details rather than rediscovering a semantic scaffold from scratch.

We ran REPA on top of our baseline PRX training, using two frozen teachers: DINOv2 and DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025). The pattern was very consistent: adding alignment improves quality metrics, and the stronger teacher helps more, at the cost of a bit of speed.

On the quality metrics, both teachers improve over the baseline. The effect is strongest with DINOv3, which achieves the best overall numbers in this run.

REPA is not free: we pay for an extra frozen teacher forward and the patch-level similarity loss, which shows up as a throughput drop from 3.95 batches/s to 3.66 (DINOv2) or 3.46 (DINOv3). In other words, DINOv3 prioritizes maximum representation quality at the cost of slower training, while DINOv2 offers a more efficient tradeoff, still delivering substantial gains with a smaller slowdown.

Our practical takeaway is that REPA is a strong lever for text-to-image training. In our setup, the throughput trade-off is real and the net speedup (time required to reach a given level of image quality) felt a bit less dramatic than what the authors of the paper report on ImageNet-style, class-conditioned generation. That said, the quality gains are still clearly significant. Qualitatively, we also saw the difference early: after ~100K steps, samples trained with alignment tended to lock in cleaner global structure and more coherent layouts, which makes it easy to see why REPA (and alignment variants more broadly) have become a go-to ingredient in modern T2I training recipes.

A natural follow-up to REPA is: what exactly should we be aligning? iREPA argues that the answer is spatial structure, not global semantics. Across a large sweep of 27 vision encoders, the authors find that ImageNet-style “global” quality (e.g., linear-probe accuracy on patch tokens) is only weakly predictive of downstream generation quality under REPA, while simple measures of patch-token spatial self-similarity correlate much more strongly with FID. Based on that diagnosis, iREPA makes two tiny but targeted changes to the REPA recipe to better preserve and transfer spatial information:

Despite representing “less than 4 lines of code”, these tweaks consistently speed up convergence and improve quality across encoders, model sizes, and even REPA-adjacent training recipes.

In our setup, we observed a similar kind of boost when applying the iREPA spatial tweaks on top of DINOv2: convergence was a bit smoother and the metrics improved more steadily over the first 100K steps. Interestingly, the same changes did not transfer as cleanly when applied on top of a DINOv3 teacher and they tended to degrade performance rather than help. We do not want to over-interpret that result: this could easily be an interaction with our specific architecture, resolution/patching, loss weighting, or even small implementation details. Still, given this inconsistency across teachers, we will likely not include these tweaks in our default recipe, even if they remain an interesting option to revisit when tuning for a specific setup.

The paper REPA Works Until It Doesn't: Early-Stopped, Holistic Alignment Supercharges Diffusion Training (Wang et al., 2025) highlights a key caveat: REPA is a powerful early accelerator, but it can plateau or even become a brake later in training. The authors describe a capacity mismatch. Once the generative model starts fitting the full data distribution (especially high-frequency details), forcing it to stay close to a frozen recognition encoder’s lower-dimensional embedding manifold becomes constraining. Their practical takeaway is simple: keep alignment for the “burn-in” phase, then turn it off with a stage-wise schedule.

We observed the same qualitative pattern in our own runs. When training our preview model, removing REPA after ~200K steps noticeably improved the overall feel of image quality, textures, micro-contrast, and fine detail continued to sharpen instead of looking slightly muted. For that reason, we also recommend treating representation alignment as a transient scaffold. Use it to get fast early progress, then drop it after a while once the model’s own generative features have caught up.

So far, “alignment” meant regularizing the generator’s internal features against a frozen teacher while treating the tokenizer / latent space as fixed. A more direct lever is to shape the latent space itself so the representation presented to the flow backbone is intrinsically easier to model, without sacrificing the reconstruction fidelity needed for editing and downstream workflows.

REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025) makes this concrete. Its starting point is a failure mode: if you simply backprop the diffusion / flow loss into the VAE, the tokenizer quickly learns a pathologically easy latent for the denoiser, which can even degrade final generation quality. REPA-E’s fix is a two-signal training recipe:

Thanks to these two tricks, the tokenizer is explicitly optimized to produce latents that yield higher alignment and empirically better generations.

In parallel, Black Forest Labs’ FLUX.2 AE work frames latent design as a trade-off between learnability, quality, and compression.Their core argument is that improving learnability requires injecting semantic structure into the representation, rather than treating the tokenizer as a pure compression module. This motivates retraining the latent space to explicitly target “better learnability and higher image quality at the same time". They do not share the full recipe, but they do clearly state the key idea: make the AE’s latent space more learnable by adding semantic or representation alignment, and explicitly point to REPA-style alignment with a frozen vision encoder as the mechanism they build on and integrate into the FLUX.2 AE.

To probe alignment in the latent space, we compared two pretrained autoencoders as drop-in tokenizers for the same flow backbone: a REPA-E-VAE (where we do add the REPA alignment objective, as in the paper) and the Flux2-AE (where we do not add REPA, following their recommendation). The results were, honestly, extremely impressive, both quantitatively and qualitatively. In samples, the gap is immediately visible: generations show more coherent global structure and cleaner layouts, with far fewer “early training” artifacts.

A first striking point is that both latent-space interventions lower the FID by ~6 points (18.20 to ~12.08), which is a much larger jump than what we typically get from “just” aligning intermediate features. This strongly supports the core idea: if the tokenizer produces a representation that is intrinsically more learnable, the flow model benefits everywhere.

The two AEs then behave quite differently in the details. Flux2-AE dominates most metrics (very low CMMD and DINO_MMD, but it comes with a huge throughput penalty: batches/sec drops from 3.95 to 1.79. In our case this slowdown is explained by practical factors they also emphasize: the model is simply heavier, and it also produces a larger latent (32 channels), which increases the amount of work the diffusion backbone has to do per step.

REPA-E-VAE is the “balanced” option: it reaches essentially the same FID as Flux2-AE while keeping throughput much closer to the baseline (3.39 batches/sec).

Architecture gets you capacity, but the training objective is what decides how that capacity is used. In practice, small changes to the loss often have outsized effects on convergence speed, conditional fidelity, and how quickly a model “locks in” global structure. In the sections below, we will go through the objectives we tested on top of our baseline rectified flow setup, starting with a simple but surprisingly effective modification: Contrastive Flow Matching.

Flow matching has a nice property in the unconditional case: trajectories are implicitly encouraged to be unique (flows should not intersect). But once we move to conditional generation (class- or text-conditioned), different conditions can still induce overlapping flows, which empirically shows up as “averaging” behavior: weaker conditional specificity, and muddier global structure. Contrastive flow matching addresses this directly by adding a contrastive term that pushes conditional flows away from other flows in the batch.

For a given training triplet (x,y,ε)(x, y, \varepsilon)(x,y,ε), standard conditional flow matching trains the model velocity vθ(xt,t,y)v_\theta(x_t,t,y)vθ​(xt​,t,y) to match the target transport direction. Contrastive flow matching keeps that positive term, but additionally samples a negative pair (x~,y~,ε~)(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}, \tilde{\varepsilon})(x~,y~​,ε~) from the batch and penalizes the model if its predicted flow is also compatible with that other trajectory. In the paper’s notation, this becomes:

LΔFM(θ)=E[∥vθ(xt,t,y)−(α˙tx+σ˙tε)∥2  −  λ∥vθ(xt,t,y)−(α˙tx~+σ˙tε~)∥2] \mathcal{L}_{\Delta \text{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\Big[ \|v_\theta(x_t,t,y)-(\dot{\alpha}_t x+\dot{\sigma}_t\varepsilon)\|^2 \;-\; \lambda \|v_\theta(x_t,t,y)-(\dot{\alpha}_t \tilde{x}+\dot{\sigma}_t\tilde{\varepsilon})\|^2 \Big] LΔFM​(θ)=E[∥vθ​(xt​,t,y)−(α˙t​x+σ˙t​ε)∥2−λ∥vθ​(xt​,t,y)−(α˙t​x~+σ˙t​ε~)∥2]

where λ∈[0,1)\lambda\in[0,1)λ∈[0,1) controls the strength of the “push-away” term. Intuitively: match your own trajectory, and be incompatible with someone else’s.

The authors show that contrastive flow matching produces more discriminative trajectories and that this translates into both quality and efficiency gains: faster convergence (reported up to 9× fewer training iterations to reach similar FID) and fewer sampling steps (reported up to 5× fewer denoising steps) on ImageNet (Deng et al. 2009) and CC3M(Sharma et al., 2018) experiments.

A key advantage is that the objective is almost a drop-in replacement: you keep the usual flow-matching loss, then add a single contrastive “push-away” term using other samples in the same batch as negatives which provides the extra supervision without introducing additional model passes.

On this run, contrastive flow matching yields a small but measurable improvement on the representation-driven metrics: CMMD goes from 0.41 → 0.40 and DINO-MMD from 0.39 → 0.36. The magnitude of the gain is smaller than what the paper reports on ImageNet, which is not too surprising: text conditioning is much more complex than discrete classes, and the training data distribution is likely less “separable” than ImageNet, making the contrastive signal harder to exploit.

We do not see an improvement in FID in this specific experiment (it slightly worsens), but the throughput cost is negligible in practice (3.95 → 3.75 batches/sec). Given the simplicity of the change and the consistent movement in the right direction for the conditioning/representation metrics, we will likely still keep contrastive flow matching in our training pipeline as a low-cost regularizer.

Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise is probably one of our favorite recent papers in the diffusion space because it is not a new trick but a reset: stop asking the network to predict off-manifold quantities (noise or velocity) and just let it denoise. Most modern diffusion and flow models train the network to predict noise ε\varepsilonε or a mixed quantity like velocity vvv. Under the manifold assumption, natural images live on a low-dimensional manifold, while ε\varepsilonε and vvv are inherently off-manifold, so predicting them can be a harder learning problem than it looks.

The authors frame the problem with the standard linear interpolation between the clean image xxx and the noise ε\varepsilonε: zt=t x+(1−t) ε, z_t = t\,x + (1-t)\,\varepsilon, zt​=tx+(1−t)ε, and the corresponding flow velocity: v=dztdt=x−ε. v = \frac{d z_t}{dt} = x - \varepsilon. v=dtdzt​​=x−ε.

Instead of outputting vθv_\thetavθ​ directly, the model predicts a clean image estimate: xθ(zt,t):=netθ(zt,t), x_\theta(z_t,t) := \mathrm{net}_\theta(z_t,t), xθ​(zt​,t):=netθ​(zt​,t), and we convert it to a velocity prediction via: vθ(zt,t)=xθ(zt,t)−zt1−t. v_\theta(z_t,t) = \frac{x_\theta(z_t,t) - z_t}{1-t}. vθ​(zt​,t)=1−txθ​(zt​,t)−zt​​.

Then we can keep the exact same flow-style objective in v-space: Lv=Et,x,ε[∥vθ(zt,t)−v∥22]withv=x−ε. \mathcal{L}_{v} = \mathbb{E}_{t,x,\varepsilon}\left[\left\|v_\theta(z_t,t) - v\right\|_2^2\right] \quad\text{with}\quad v = x-\varepsilon. Lv​=Et,x,ε​[∥vθ​(zt​,t)−v∥22​]withv=x−ε.

This formulation makes the learning problem substantially easier in high dimensions: instead of predicting noise or velocity (which are essentially unconstrained in pixel space), the network predicts the clean image xxx, i.e., something that lies on the data manifold. In practice, this makes it feasible to train large-patch Transformers directly on pixels without a VAE or tokenizer while keeping optimization stable and the total number of tokens manageable.

We first evaluated x-prediction in the same setting as the rest of our objective experiments, namely training in the FLUX latent space at 256×256 resolution.

In this regime, the benefit of x-prediction is unclear. While FID improves slightly compared to the baseline, both CMMD and DINO-MMD degrade noticeably, and throughput is unchanged. This suggests that, when working in an already well-structured latent space, predicting clean images instead of velocity does not consistently dominate the baseline objective, and can even hurt representation-level alignment.

That said, this experiment is not where x-prediction really shines.

The exciting part is that x-prediction stabilizes high-dimensional training, making it feasible to use larger patches and denoise directly in pixel space, without a VAE, at much higher resolutions. Using JiT, we trained a model directly on 1024×1024 images with 32×32 patches, instead of operating in a compressed latent space. Despite the much higher resolution and the absence of a tokenizer, optimization remained stable and fast. We reached FID 17.42, DINO_MMD 0.56, and CMMD 0.71 with a throughput of 1.33 batches/sec.

These results are remarkable: training directly on 1024×1024 images is only about 3× slower than training in a 256×256 latent space, while operating on raw pixels. This strongly supports the core claim of Back to Basics: letting the model predict clean images makes the learning problem significantly easier, and opens the door to high-resolution, tokenizer-free text-to-image training without prohibitive compute costs.

As a result, we plan to use this formulation as the backbone of our upcoming speedrun experiments, to see how far we can push it when combined with the other efficiency and sparsification techniques discussed above. The main downside for now is that this approach does not let us benefit from the very nice properties of the FLUX.2 VAE; exploring whether some form of alignment or hybrid training could make these two worlds compatible is an open direction we plan to investigate further.

So far, most of the techniques we discussed focus on making each training step more effective: improving the objective, shaping the representations, or accelerating convergence. The next lever is orthogonal: make each step cheaper.

For diffusion and flow transformers, the dominant cost is running deep transformer stacks over a large set of image/latent tokens where attention scales poorly with sequence length. Token sparsification methods target this directly by ensuring that only a subset of tokens pays the full compute price in the expensive parts of the network, while still preserving enough information flow to keep quality high.Most masking approaches accelerate training by removing tokens from the forward pass, then asking the model to hallucinate the missing content from learned placeholders. That works surprisingly well, but it violates the spirit of iterative denoising. Instead of refining all the content in each step, we are reconstructing parts from scratch.

Two recent papers illustrate a cleaner alternative: instead of deleting information, they reorganize where compute is spent. TREAD and SPRINT share the same high-level objective of avoiding full-depth computation for every token at every layer, but they pursue it through complementary strategies.

TREAD's (Krause et al., 2025) core idea is to replace compute reduction through information loss, such as dropping or masking tokens, with compute reduction through information transport using token routing. It introduces a route: for each training sample, it randomly selects a fraction of tokens and temporarily bypasses a contiguous chunk of layers, then re-injects those tokens later. Tokens are not discarded. Instead, they avoid paying the cost of full depth. Concretely, for a denoiser with a stack of blocks L0,…,LB−1L_0, \dots, L_{B-1}L0​,…,LB−1​, TREAD defines a route ritojr_{i\\to j}ritoj​ (start layer iii, end layer jjj). A subset of tokens follows the cheap path (identity) across Li,…,LjL_i,\dots,L_jLi​,…,Lj​, while the rest follows the normal full computation. Then both streams merge again at LjL_jLj​. In practice, the paper shows that routing up to 50% of tokens remains effective, while higher rates begin to degrade quality.

SPRINT (Park et al., 2025) extends this approach by introducing sparsity in the most computationally expensive parts of the network, while preserving a dense information pathway. Its recipe is intentionally structured: run dense early layers over all tokens to build reliable low-level features, then keep only a subset of tokens through the sparse middle layers where compute is heaviest, and finally go dense again by re-expanding and fusing sparse deep features with a dense residual stream from the early layers, before producing the output. The key distinction from TREAD is where robustness comes from: TREAD keeps tokens “present” but shallower (routing), whereas SPRINT allows many tokens to be absent in the middle blocks, relying on the dense residual path to preserve full-resolution information. This is what enables more aggressive sparsification in practice. The paper explores drop ratios around 75%, versus ~50% for TREAD.

Under our standard 256×256 latent setup, both methods deliver the primary benefit we were targeting. TREAD goes from 3.95 → 4.11 batches/sec, and SPRINT pushes it a bit further to 4.20 batches/sec. The cost is that under our evaluation protocol, this extra throughput comes with a clear loss in quality: FID rises from 18.20 to 21.61 (TREAD) and 22.56 (SPRINT), with the same pattern observed in CMMD and DINO-MMD.

Taken at face value, routing yields a modest ~7–9% throughput gain, but it comes with worse metrics in this benchmark, with SPRINT (the more aggressive scheme) degrading quality slightly more than TREAD.

One important caveat is that token-sparse / routed models tend to score worse under vanilla Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), and this effect is likely amplified here because these runs are still relatively undertrained in our setting. The authors of Guiding Token-Sparse Diffusion Models (Krause et al., 2025) argue this is partly an evaluation mismatch: routing changes the model’s effective capacity, and plain “conditional vs. unconditional” CFG often becomes less effective, which can artificially reduce quality. We deliberately did not use specialized guidance schemes to keep our benchmark consistent across methods, and at this stage it would also not be very meaningful to treat the sparse model as a “bad version of itself” for guidance. As a result, we consider these numbers directionally useful, but still pessimistic and worth interpreting with caution.

At 256×256, routing only gave modest gains because the model processes relatively few tokens. At 1024×1024, the picture changes completely. With 1024 tokens, routing finally targets the dominant cost, and the results are striking.

Both TREAD and SPRINT deliver large throughput gains over the dense baseline, with SPRINT pushing speed the furthest. More importantly, this time the gains do not come at the expense of quality but quite the opposite. TREAD in particular stands out, with a dramatic drop in FID (17.42 → 14.10) alongside strong improvements in CMMD and DINO-MMD. SPRINT is slightly more aggressive and a bit noisier in quality, but still clearly improves over the baseline while being the fastest option.

In short, this is the regime where token routing really shines: high resolution, many tokens, and JiT-style pixel-space training. Here, routing is no longer a marginal optimization—it’s a major lever that improves both how fast and how well the model trains.

After covering representation alignment, the core training objective, and token routing, we turned to the fourth axis that kept constantly mattered in practice: data. We found that the choice of training data, including how it is described through captions, can influence the trajectory of a training run as much as optimization techniques. Below are three concrete data experiments that consistently moved the needle in our setup.

Captions are an essential part of the training set: for a text-to-image model, they are not just metadata, they are the supervision. The DALL·E 3 (Betker et al., 2023) research paper showed that richer captions can be one of the strongest levers for improving training signal and prompt-following. To isolate the effect in our setup, we kept everything else fixed and changed only the caption style to compare:

Long, descriptive captions (our baseline): multi-clause captions that mention composition, attributes, lighting, materials, and relationships.

Example "A photograph depicts a fluffy lop-eared rabbit sitting on a weathered wooden surface outdoors. The rabbit is predominantly white with patches of light brown and tan fur, particularly on its head and ears. Its ears droop noticeably, and its fur appears soft and thick. The rabbit's eyes are dark and expressive. It is positioned slightly off-center, facing towards the left of the frame. Behind the rabbit, slightly out of focus, is a miniature dark red metal wheelbarrow. A partially visible orange apple sits to the left of the rabbit. Fallen autumn leaves, predominantly reddish-brown, are scattered around the rabbit and apple on the wooden surface. The background is a blurred but visible expanse of green grass, suggesting an outdoor setting. The lighting is soft and natural, likely diffused daylight, casting no harsh shadows. The overall atmosphere is calm, peaceful, and autumnal. The aesthetic is rustic and charming, with a focus on the rabbit as the main subject. The color palette is muted and natural, consisting mainly of whites, browns, oranges, and greens. The style is naturalistic and straightforward, without any overt artistic manipulation. The vibe is gentle and heartwarming."

Short, one-line captions: minimal descriptions with much less structure.

Example "A rabbit sitting on top of a wooden table."

The outcome was unambiguous: switching to short captions severely hurt convergence across all metrics. Long captions provide a richer supervision signal: beyond prompt adherence, there is a very practical optimization reason. More tokens usually means more information, and therefore more learning signal for the denoiser. When the conditioning text specifies composition, attributes, lighting, materials, and relationships, the model gets a sharper “target” for what the denoising trajectory should preserve and refine, especially early in training.

The fun paradox is that this extra detail often makes the learning problem easier, not harder: intuitively, one might expect longer prompts, with more attributes, constraints, and relationships, to increase complexity and burden the model. In practice, the opposite happens. Short captions leave many degrees of freedom unspecified, forcing the model to learn under ambiguity and implicitly average across multiple plausible interpretations. Long captions collapse that uncertainty by turning implicit choices into explicit constraints, allowing the denoiser to focus its capacity on refining a well-posed solution instead of guessing what matters.

Long captions are a strong training-time accelerator, but we still want the model to behave well on short prompts because that is how people actually use these systems. A simple workaround is to end training with a short fine-tuning stage on a mixture of long and short captions. That keeps the benefits of rich supervision early, while teaching the model to stay robust when conditioning is sparse.

Another data-related research question we explore is whether a low-cost synthetic corpus can accelerate early training compared to a real corpus of similar size. For this benchmark, we trained a model on a dataset of real images collected from Pexels and compared it with our Baseline which was trained on synthetic data generated with MidjourneyV6, both of which have around 1M images. We evaluated both runs against the same Unsplash reference set, composed exclusively of real images.

The synthetic-trained model scores better on CMMD and DINO-MMD, while the model trained on real images achieves a lower FID. Rather than a contradiction, this split mostly reflects what these metrics emphasize.

FID is particularly sensitive to low-level image statistics: fine textures, high-frequency detail, noise patterns, and the subtle irregularities of real photography. Since our evaluation reference is composed of real images, a model trained on real photos naturally matches those statistics more closely, which translates into a better FID. Synthetic images, by contrast, often exhibit slightly different high-frequency signatures, cleaner edges, smoother micro-textures, more uniform noise, which are barely noticeable qualitatively but still get penalized by distributional metrics like FID.

Qualitatively, this difference is easy to spot. Models trained on synthetic data tend to produce images with cleaner global structure and stronger compositional and object coherence, but also exhibit a more synthetic appearance, characterized by smoother textures and reduced photographic noise. In contrast, models trained on real images better capture the irregular, fine-grained textures typical of natural photographs, though they often require more training to achieve comparable global structure.

One plausible explanation synthetic data remains so effective early on is that it exposes the model to a wider range of compositional collisions: unusual pairings of objects, attributes, styles, and viewpoints that rarely co-occur in natural datasets. While this can hurt realism at the texture level, it forces the model to explain a broader space of combinations, which appears to help with early disentanglement and structure learning.

Considered jointly, this suggests a simple but practical strategy: synthetic data is an efficient way to bootstrap training and lock in global structure quickly, while real images remain important later on if matching photographic texture statistics is the priority.

Finally, we experimented with a targeted Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) pass using Alchemist (Startsev et al., 2025), a compact dataset explicitly curated for high-impact. Alchemist is small by design (3,350 image–text pairs), but is constructed through a sophisticated curation pipeline that starts from a web-scale pool and progressively distills it down to visually exceptional samples.

In our setup, we fine-tuned our preview models for 20K steps on Alchemist. Despite the dataset’s small size, it had an outsized effect: it adds a distinct “style layer” with better composition, more photographic polish, and richer scenes without a clear impact on generalization.

The samples below show a side-by-side comparison of generations from the same base model, before and after the Alchemist fine-tuning pass.

Last but not least, we will briefly cover two practical training details that turned out to matter more than we expected. These factors are easily overlooked and in our case they had a clear impact on convergence and final image quality.

We generally default to AdamW for our benchmarks because it’s predictable and easy to compare across runs. However, lately, we have seen a renewed interest in optimizers that try to behave more like a good preconditioner without the full overhead of second-order methods. One recent example is Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), which, at a high level, tries to improve optimization by applying a better-conditioned update step, often translating into faster convergence and cleaner progress early in training.

In our setup, Muon was one of the rare cases in which a change of optimizer produced an immediately observable effect on the metrics.

For this experiment, we used the official PyTorch implementation of Muon, which at the moment supports Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) training only. If you’re running Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP), there are community variants available; for example here.

While we refrain from broad conclusions based on a single benchmark, these results indicate that optimizer choice extends beyond stability considerations and can yield tangible gains in time-to-quality.

We eventually identified an error in our setup, where the denoiser weights were mistakenly stored in bfloat16 for a period of time.

To be clear, using the BF16 autocast is great. Running the forward and backward passes in BF16 or mixed precision is standard and usually what you want for speed and memory. The problem arises from keeping the parameters in BF16 precision, which negatively impacts numerically sensitive operations.

In practice, some layers and operations are much less tolerant to reduced parameter precision:

So the rule we now follow very strictly is: use BF16 autocast for compute, but keep weights (and optimizer state) in FP32 or at least ensure numerically sensitive modules stay FP32.

It is not a glamorous trick but it is exactly the kind of “silent” detail that can cost you multiple days of work if you do not notice it early.

We ran a systematic set of ablations on PRX training, comparing a range of optimization, representation, efficiency, and data choices against a clean flow-matching baseline using both quality metrics and throughput.

The biggest gains came from alignment: REPA boosts early convergence (best used as a burn-in, then turned off), and better latents/tokenizers (REPA-E/FLUX2-AE) give a large jump in quality with clear speed trade-offs. Objective tweaks were mixed—contrastive FM helped slightly, while x-prediction mattered most by enabling stable 1024² pixel training. Token routing (TREAD/SPRINT) is minor at 256² but becomes a major win at high resolution. Data and practical details also mattered: long captions are critical, synthetic vs. real data shifts texture vs. structure, small SFT adds polish, Muon helped, and BF16-stored weights quietly hurt training.

That’s it for Part 2! If you want to play with an earlier public checkpoint from this series, the PRX-1024 T2I beta is still available here.

We are really excited about what’s next: in the coming weeks we will release the full source code of the PRX training framework, and we will do a public 24-hour “speedrun” where we combine the best ideas from this post into a single run and see how far the full recipe can go in one day.

If you made it this far, first of all thank you very much for your interest. Furthermore, we would love to have you join our Discord community where we discuss PRX progress and results, along with everything related to diffusion and text-to-image models.

Amazing work ! Super nice to see you work on this !

Carbon dioxide-spilling converted turbines have been installed in a Mississippi xAI data center despite the known health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk's xAI is using eight converted jet engine turbines to power a Mississippi data center. While the generators have the required state-level permission and permits, there remain concerns about the impact they could have on the local environment. The permits allow for a 25% higher limit in pollutants known as volatile organic compounds, but those compounds, paired with the expulsion of carbon monoxide, have environmentalists warning that the use of jet engines to power data centers is a step in the wrong direction. The New York Times reports that the Southern Environmental Law Center has already challenged Mississippi's decision to approve the turbines for use at xAI's data center.

The group argues that xAI has failed to provide guarantees that the jet-powered turbines meet emissions standards for specific pollutants, including formaldehyde. It also accuses xAI of what the report terms the "undercounting" of projected emissions in relation to the data center's power sources. This comes after the same group sued xAI over its use of gas generators without the required permits in an area with more than 100,000 inhabitants.

The generators used by xAI are converted by ProEnergy, a Missouri-based outfit that repurposes the unused General Electric turbines that are typically found attached to Boeing airplanes. The company was quick to turn its attention to the possibility of using the jet engines to power data centers after it was identified that the demand for energy was outpacing the ability of traditional utility companies to keep up. Each turbine is capable of producing up to 50 megawatts of electricity. Normally, that would be enough to keep around 15,000 homes up and running.

The availability of energy has long been an issue for data centers, both existing and those still on the drawing board. A July 2026 report predicted that data centers would use 20% of all U.S. power by 2035, a figure that was a huge 83% increase over the same forecast that was made seven months prior. Despite that news, as of April this year, half of data center buildouts had been canceled or delayed due to, among other things, a lack of power. This is an issue for xAI especially, with Musk saying in August that xAI would increase its data center capacity by 7x before the end of 2027. Delays and cancelations have the potential to derail those plans.

Public sentiment around data centers has turned sour in recent months amid power issues and concerns over how much water these facilities use. While using converted jet engines could potentially help with one issue, it seems unlikely that the pollution they generate will help assuage the concerns of locals anytime soon.

#10307. Redmagic 12 Pro review: You’ve never gamed on a phone like this before

The Redmagic 12 Pro impresses with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, liquid cooling, a fan, plus a massive 8,400mAh battery to keep the games going for hours and hours.

As I sat in my living room with my family, playing Monster Hunter Outlanders together on the Redmagic 12 Pro, I completely forgot I was playing on a phone. The game looked perfect. It ran at a locked 60FPS and hadn’t dropped frames since I began playing over an hour ago. It just felt like I was back in college, playing Monster Hunter Freedom on my PSP with my friends in the same room.

Most other phones at this point would have throttled hard. What began at 60FPS almost certainly would have been 40FPS tops after 30 minutes or so; the frame drops during heavy fights would have been even worse, but the Redmagic 12 Pro didn’t skip a beat. Even after a solid hour of playing, the battery had only dropped 10%, completely erasing all concerns about using my phone as a gaming console.

This thing is the real deal, and while I’ve used plenty of high-performance phones and gaming phones over the years, none have quite nailed it as this one has. Now, with my Redmagic 12 Pro and my trusty GameSir G8 Galileo, I can game whenever and wherever I want without battery anxiety or thermal problems. Redmagic has gotten really good at this gaming thing.

Sustained gaming performance is difficult to pull off on a phone, which is why the Redmagic 12 Pro features two types of active cooling: a fan and liquid cooling. This design builds on last year’s with a larger liquid cooling system and a more efficient fan. The intake and exhaust vents are on the sides of the phone, not the back, ensuring these shouldn’t get easily blocked. Despite this, the phone is IP68 and IP69 rated.

Most modern phones have huge camera islands that make them awkward to use in controllers, but the Redmagic 12 Pro features a completely flat build that fits perfectly in *any* controller. I don’t usually like overly flat builds, but it actually suits this phone’s purpose.

This should mean the phone does exceedingly well in benchmarks, but I have the distinct feeling the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor inside is making that overly difficult. I don’t have any other SD8 Elite Gen 6 phones just yet, but rumor has it that this is one *hot* chipset. I saw the phone hit 50C during testing, so that definitely seems to be the case.

In 3DMark Solar Bay Extreme, a benchmark that stresses ray-tracing performance over 20 minutes, the Redmagic 12 Pro started at 2065 points and ended at 1169 on its last run. That’s a 43% drop in performance over a 20-minute period, which is in line with passively-cooled phones like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Regardless, the initial performance is nearly double the S26 Ultra, while the 1169 end score matches the S26 Ultra’s best score and is roughly 35% higher than the S26 Ultra’s sustained performance score of around 860.

Actual gaming seemed to fare better in my testing, where I saw sustained performance consistently outperform any Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone I have in my possession. When running Wanderstop through the phone’s built-in Steam emulation (more on that soon), the Redmagic 12 Pro averaged 72FPS at the highest settings. Other phones with SD8 Elite Gen 5 processors scored half that, at best. Native Android games like Monster Hunter Outlanders worked even better.

But it’s not just performance that sets this phone apart; it’s the gaming features. Redmagic has fully leaned into the mobile gaming power user angle with its software. Pressing and holding the red button on the right side of the phone launches Gravity X, the built-in game launcher that keeps all your games in one place. It even features an embedded Steam emulator, so all you need to do is sign in with your Steam account and download anything in your library.

Overall performance on Steam games is impressive, but like any emulation, not everything is going to work. Hogwarts Legacy worked near-flawlessly at medium settings, but titles like Star Wars Galactic Racer wouldn’t run at all. Other apps that run Steam games, like DroidDeck and Game Native, also work, but the Adreno 850 GPU doesn’t have official support on those apps yet, so compatibility is very hit or miss (mostly miss) for now.

The Redmagic 12 Pro’s in-game menu is also unlike anything you’ve ever seen. It’s not just jam-packed with information, but has a boatload of bespoke features. One custom mapping tool lets you map the triggers (yes, this phone has capacitive triggers on the side) to any on-screen virtual key.

Another utility records all the time, Xbox/PS5/Switch style, and saves a clip at the touch of a floating button. Yet another features on on-screen AI anime character that can interact with your games and even give you gameplay feedback. You can even enable frame gen and Super Resolution in any game. It’s wild.

All this is wrapped up in an incredibly impressive hardware package, with loud, clear speakers, an excellent 185Hz AMOLED display (that uses DC dimming and 2160Hz PWM for eye comfort), with 5,000-nit peak brightness. I measured the actual HDR brightness at 2300-nits, so this can get nice and bright when it needs to.

If there was ever a phone that could play games and still get you through a full day’s normal phone usage, it’s this one. Passthrough charging is also supported, too, so you can keep the battery from getting overcharged or overheated while gaming for hours.

As is the case with many laser-focused devices like this, the camera is the low point of the experience. It’s got a 50MP rear camera and a 50MP ultra wide. Both get the job done, but they’ll never impress you.

The 16MP 9th-generation under display camera looks impressive on the surface — you can’t see it at all, even with light shining off the display — but the results are still far from good. Redmagic uses an AI algorithm to substantially enhance the overall quality, which cleans up the image nicely but exhibits lots of hallucinations. Just look at my eyes in the above picture. It’s not good.

Thankfully, the Android 17-based Redmagic OS 12 software is quite good. Visually, it reminds me of a mix of AOSP and Samsung’s One UI. Lots of expected features are here — an AI wallpaper generator, call screening, recording with transcripts, writing help, etc — plus all the awesome gaming-focused tools and quite a bit of customization across the OS.

It’s a great overall experience, but Redmagic only offers software updates for 3 years, so this one won’t stay around as long as some other phones. If you’re more interested in mobile gaming than anything — especially if you want a phone that can easily run Steam games in addition to mobile stuff — this is an impressively good choice.

Intel Foundry last week made available its Intel 14A process design kit (PDK) version 0.9, an important milestone in the development of this next-generation manufacturing technology. The company says that the production node is reaching performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, and the results are backed by silicon validation. Intel plans to release PDK 1.0 in the first quarter of 2027, which will validate the technology's readiness for high-volume manufacturing (HVM).

A process design kit contains transistor models, design rules, and other information that enables chip designers to develop products for a particular manufacturing process using electronic design automation (EDA) tools. The accuracy and quality of the PDK are crucial for modelling how chips will perform once manufactured, and the release of PDK 0.9 is particularly important because it provides customers with a representation of Intel 14A based on actual silicon measurements rather than on theoretical models or simulations. At this stage, customers can proceed with product development with greater confidence that the technology will meet their requirements when it comes to performance and power consumption.

Intel says that PDK 0.9 lets customers develop designs intended to enter risk production around the time the process is certified, which — provided that PDK accurately reflects the characteristics of manufactured silicon — in many cases enables chip developers to greatly reduce the number of silicon revisions between initial tapeout and mass production. Of course, availability of PDK 0.9 does not indicate that Intel 14A is ready or even close to mass production, as the company expects to validate HVM readiness only with PDK 1.0, sometime in Q1 2027. Again, this does not mean that 14A will enter mass production in early 2027, as Intel itself expects to begin mass production using its 14A process technology in 2028, following risk production for its own products in the second half of 2027.

"From a customer perspective, the PDK 0.9 gives customers the confidence to design products on Intel 14A, as the technology is reaching the industry-standard performance and yield maturity expected at this stage of development, supported by silicon-backed validation," said Ben Sell, corporate vice president and general manager of front-end technology development at Intel Foundry.

Intel 14A builds on top of architectural foundations introduced with Intel 18A but incorporates several substantial enhancements. These include 2nd Generation RibbonFET 2 gate-all-around (GAA) transistors, PowerDirect backside power delivery (which delivers power right to the transistor source/drain regions without using intermediate connections like TSVs used by PowerVia), and Turbo Cells (high-performance standard cells designed to accelerate timing-critical paths in CPUs and GPUs), which provide chip designers with additional ways to increase performance and optimize power efficiency. Since Intel has previously outlined advantages of these technologies, the latest announcement does not provide updates regarding transistor performance, power consumption, or transistor density figures for Intel 14A.

Beyond improvements to transistor, power delivery, and interconnect technologies, Intel is applying manufacturing experience gained during 12 months of Intel 18A production to accelerate maturation of 14A. Specifically, the company says it has increased investments in inline defect detection, modeling, and simulation to identify potential manufacturing problems earlier in the development cycle. These initiatives are intended to improve manufacturing yields, process variability, ultimately transistor performance, and reduce production cycle times. Intel also says it has introduced several strategic initiatives to accelerate technology development, although it does not quantify their impact.

Another important change concerns Intel's relationships with equipment and materials suppliers. The company says it has revised its collaboration model to involve technology development teams and external suppliers earlier in the process development cycle. The goal of such close collaborations is to address manufacturing defects and improve equipment capabilities before they become obstacles for yield improvements after the technology enters mass production. Intel also conducts regular yield summit meetings with suppliers to accelerate progress on critical development objectives.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

"This has required evolving our collaboration model with equipment and material suppliers, and earlier engagement from our [technology development] leaders with suppliers to drive improvements in defects and equipment capabilities," Sell said.

A bonus of such early collaboration is that equipment and materials suppliers may incorporate Intel's requirements into their standard products and development roadmaps. This could give Intel an advantage over competitors, which would have to either adapt their manufacturing processes to equipment optimized around Intel's requirements or work with suppliers to develop alternative solutions from scratch.

Historically, Intel frequently set the direction for semiconductor manufacturing technologies as other chipmakers subsequently adopted similar approaches. One notable exception was immersion DUV lithography, which Intel adopted after TSMC, which led the development of immersion DUV lithography. By engaging equipment and materials suppliers earlier, Intel could regain some of its historical influence over the development of industry-standard manufacturing solutions, though the importance of this should not be overestimated.

Meanwhile, Intel continues to expand the design ecosystem for its 14A technology. Cadence and Intel have established a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) collaboration focused on next-generation AI-driven design tools and intellectual property, whereas Keysight, Siemens, and Synopsys have announced design-tool certifications for the process. Intel is also working with other software developers and IP providers to validate design flows and reusable building blocks required by prospective foundry customers.

Intel says it is encouraged by customer feedback regarding the progress of 14A development. However, the company has not identified any customers that have committed to manufacturing products using the technology, disclosed customer tape-outs, or announced specific manufacturing agreements, which is normal for the foundry industry. For Intel Foundry, attracting external customers remains particularly important because development costs of modern leading-edge process technologies can only be recoupled when they are used to make hundreds of millions of chips, way more than Intel sells these days. Meanwhile, the commercial success of Intel Foundry with advanced manufacturing technologies depends not only on transistor performance and manufacturing yields, but also on its ability to deliver predictable development schedules.

Looking ahead, Intel intends to continue improving performance, yields, variability, and manufacturing cycle times of 14A, though for now the company does not disclose any actual goals. Intel also plans additional process enhancements and performance refinements for 14A-E and 14A-P nodes after the initial technology becomes available. However, exact schedules for these nodes are not known at the moment.

"Our next major milestone is the Intel 14A PDK 1.0, expected in the first quarter of 2027," said Ali Farhang, corporate vice president and general manager of Intel Foundry's design technology platform organization. "I am looking forward to sustaining this level of quality across future releases and continuing to earn our customers' trust by delivering on our commitments with a customer-first mindset."

This move could help data centers operate sooner without waiting for the rest of the grid to catch up to its peak demand.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Electricity consumption is one of the biggest concerns that residents bring up whenever a data center is proposed in their community, which is why OpenAI is taking steps to minimize its impact on the local electricity grid. According to the company, its Grid Protectors Program aims to reduce the power consumption of its data centers as local demand increases, ensuring that the grid is not overwhelmed during peak hours. Aside from ensuring that the lights remain on for everyone, it would also allow its data centers to connect to the grid and go online sooner instead of waiting for the additional power sources to come online.

“Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most,” OpenAI said in its blog. It also added, “Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.”

OpenAI is testing the program in its planned Effingham County campus in Georgia, with the company saying that it has already signed a 3.2-gigawatt agreement with Georgia Power that included 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response. This ensures that if demand jumps on the hottest days of the year, there would be enough power to accommodate the hundreds of thousands of air conditioners keeping Georgians cool. With the average American home drawing around 1,200 kilowatts, the 1,000-megawatt buffer is more than enough to power around 800,000 households — nearly 20% of the state’s homes.

This technology, called demand response, has been around for decades now, where large operators reduce their demand in response to a peak in demand from other consumers. Before automation, grid operators would manually call up industrial customers like steel mills and ask them to cut consumption to ensure the reliability of the entire grid. But with modern technologies and IoT, it can now be done automatically, allowing data centers to reduce their load in under a minute. In fact, Nvidia has already been experimenting with a similar system in the UK and has proven that it works.

Microsoft's claimed performance gains will need to be tested

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following a resurgence of 8GB RAM laptops earlier this year, and in the wake of promises to improve Windows 11 performance using just 8GB of RAM, Microsoft has today announced what it claims are a series of performance improvements. Driven by an ongoing global PC component shortage that is forcing manufacturers to dumb down specs, the company says that with 8GB of RAM, Windows is now 20% more responsive and 40% faster when it comes to multitasking.

The development shared today by Microsoft is an update to a commitment earlier this year to improve the quality and performance of Windows 11, a major bugbear of users since its launch. Microsoft says it has taken a three-pronged approach to memory optimization: making better use of memory in Windows 11 PCs, protecting interactions that need to feel instant, and ensuring key apps and Windows use less memory. While the company admits you'll be able to do more on 16GB or 32GB of RAM, it says "we're making sure you can do more, even with 8GB."

The headline performance gain is a claim that Windows is now up to 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs. Likewise, multitasking is now purportedly 40% faster in Microsoft's lab tests. Of course, these are internal tests conducted in favorable conditions by Microsoft.

Microsoft says it has tuned compression for useful apps and data, and can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory, rather than moving it to storage. In practice, this should mean that apps and tabs left open should be less likely to reload when you go back to them.

The claim of 20% more responsiveness specifically relates to tasks like opening Start, searching, right-clicking, opening Settings, using the Snipping Tool, and opening File Explorer. The company says it has achieved this by backing off background tasks like indexing while you're using your PC actively. Edge now reportedly opens up to 33% faster. There's also an Efficiency Mode for Microsoft Teams, which can be set to on by default, improving launch times by 20%.

Microsoft says that its claims of 40% speed boosts to multitasking are based on a demanding workflow of 20 Microsoft Edge Tabs, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, Outlook, and File Explorer all being opened one after the other.

Other improvements include reducing committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB in apps like Microsoft Edge and 365 apps, and reducing the memory footprint of Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook by 360MB. Third-party apps can also benefit from improved memory management, with Microsoft stating WhatsApp is already taking advantage.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Moving forward, Microsoft says it has plans to make memory compression even smarter and more efficient. Windows features and apps will share common parts, such as Search and Widgets using one web Engine, for instance. WinUI 3 apps like File Explorer and Notepad will be designed to use less memory and open faster, and Microsoft is working with PC makers and silicon manufacturers to reduce how much memory a PC needs to hold in reserve to support its hardware, making more space for Windows.
